utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. I would like the registrar to call out the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. IT-95-13a-T, the Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Niemann, and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi, and Mr. Vos for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Good morning, my name is Tomas Fila. I appear with my colleagues Mr. Petrovic and Mr. Kostic, council for the accused Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, can you hear me well. Is your language accessible to you? Thank you. Before we start, let us deal briefly with a few housekeeping matters. First of all, we thought -- I start with minor problems. We thought we can do without the appearances so as to save time, and for this purpose, I would assume that if there are no changes in the various teams, the Prosecution and Defence teams, we take it for granted that the stenographers will write down the usual names unless, as I say, we are warned by one of the teams and there will be changes to be recorded. Let us now -- a second small matter. Two witness statements are missing in our files, and the statements by Mr. Melitic vis Sejlaslav (phoen) and the statement by Mr. Nikulavic (phoen) Dusan. No judge has been able to find those statements. Yes, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. We haven't taken their statements because we brought them in all of a sudden, so to speak, but their testimonies will be very brief. They have to do with two hours only, and they're not related to Vukovar, so perhaps if our time is running out, then perhaps the Prosecutor and we can have a look at this and we can agree on it without contesting it after seeing the video, so it is two hours altogether. There won't be any problems, really. You will see, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We'll just have to have a discussion, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Another problem, I understand the Prosecutor has no objection to adding two witnesses to the list of witnesses to be heard through video link next Monday, if this is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will issue an order today, that it is accepted, the motion by the Defence has been then granted. Before we move on again briefly to our court schedule, I would like to raise a problem again with the parties. We thought we should, of course, if the parties are agreeable, we might or we apply some new Rules of Procedure which are likely to be adopted pretty soon by the Plenary of all Judges, and this is about sentencing. Now, one Rule can be read as follows: "The parties" -- this is about the presentation of evidence -- and "parties may present evidence at the trial including any relevant information that may assist the Trial Chamber in determining an appropriate sentence if the accused is found guilty on one or more of the charges in the indictment." So I will read it again: "The parties may present evidence on any relevant information that may assist the Trial Chamber in determining an appropriate sentence if the accused is found guilty on one or more of the charges in the indictment." Another Rule would provide as follows: It's a Rule about closing arguments by the parties: "The parties shall also address in their closing arguments matters of sentencing in closing arguments." So the parties shall also address matters of sentencing in closing arguments. Of course, this would be Rules which apply in any case, even if eventually the accused is acquitted. I stress this point. So this, of course, is regardless of whether or not then eventually the accused is acquitted or convicted. I wonder whether -- so we would be pleased to apply these provisions which are not yet binding which are likely to become a set of Rules of Procedure and Evidence, but, of course, we would like to have the agreement of the parties. So I wonder whether Mr. Fila would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am one of the members of the team that actually proposed this, so I have to agree with what I had proposed myself. Thank you. I'm sorry, Your Honour. Just one more thing. I think that if we start applying this, it is impossible to do it at this particular point in time, we have to leave it until June. We simply won't have time to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, because I assume you would call additional witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. Not too many really, two or three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. That's why we are now raising this problem because I will immediately move on after hearing the Prosecutor to the court schedule for our trial. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I understand the proposed new Rule, the evidence on sentencing will be called as part of the Defence case, and then the Prosecution rebuttal to the Defence case will be something that follows after all of the close of the evidence of the Defence. If that's the case, we have no difficulty with that. The issue with respect to closing argument, we don't have any problem with that. Your Honours have asked us to put in our closing argument in writing, which we are prepared to do, happy to do. But there is one application we do make, and that is that both parties file their closing argument on the same day because we don't -- we submit that it would be inappropriate that the arguments be, in a sense, presented to the court one in reply to the other. It should be, in our submission, the views of either party submitted at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see that Mr. Fila does agree. Yes, all right. So you don't have any objection to the possible application of the new rules. The problem arises also because of the time available to us. Now, we have this week two and a half days, then the whole of next week, and then we have to start again our hearing on the 22nd of June, no longer on the date which had been scheduled. On the 22nd of June, but the advantage of that week would be that we would have five working days, from the 22nd to the 26th of June, and so I wonder whether we could -- of course, we don't want to, in any manner, restrict the rights of the Defence because without saying that -- if need be, we will go on to July, and we will see whether we can find some time, but I wonder whether it is possible for the Defence to finish the whole trial by the 26th of June, so whether you could call your own witnesses plus any witnesses on the possible sentencing? Sorry, one second. Because if we take up the suggestion as made by Mr. Niemann, we could have just one day for closing arguments, and this could be, say, Friday, the 26th of June. So morning and afternoon. So I wonder whether we could hear the evidence before the 26th of June? Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I promised, I'm going to complete all the evidence by the end of next week, and I had planned on leaving Friday for Mr. Niemann so that he could present his rebuttal case, as requested, but the new Rule that we will be applying now, perhaps we need only a day, not even an entire day, because the witnesses that will be speaking will be speaking about the character of the accused, so we don't really need that much time. I think one day is sufficient for that, the 22nd, for example. And then until Friday we can see when we are going to give each other our closing arguments because I have nine witnesses here today, Your Honour. Out of these nine witnesses, four are like the ones that you don't have their statements. We can finish this in half an hour, and if they are not contested in any way, we don't even have to hear them. We can finish with five witnesses in these two and a half days, but we will have a look at the tape and see what it's about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It depends on how long there is available in June, but it looks as though we could probably do it in that time, Your Honours. We would be reasonably optimistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tomorrow, just a few practical indications. Tomorrow, since we have to have a long break, a lunch break from a quarter to twelve to three o'clock, I would like to suggest that we should start at 9.00, if it is suitable, 9.00, and then we will have this long break, and then we go on from 3.00 to 6.00, if possible. Then on Wednesday we will start again, as usual, at 9.30 to 12.30, and then from 2.00 to 5.00 -- sorry, on Wednesday we will stop at 12.30 because, as you know, this courtroom must be made available to another Trial Chamber. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's acceptable to the Prosecution. I might just indicate at this stage that I regret that I won't be available all of that time. I have another case, a commitment on another matter, but my colleagues will be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. So we may now start with the first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jevtovic. May I ask you to stand and make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, did the investigator, the Fila legal office, Mr. Miro Lazarevic, did he talk to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Have you read this statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Have you signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is this the statement in question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is in Serbian and in English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D68 and the English translation D68A.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the statement in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If there are no objections, I suggest it be admitted into evidence as D68.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, did you graduate from the faculty of philosophy in Belgrade and did you get your MA from the faculty of political sciences in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I graduated from the faculty of political sciences and got my MA there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In 1991, were you employed in Radio Djerdap and what were you actually doing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I was director and editor in chief of Radio Djerdap.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that what you do now too?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On the 20th of November, 1991, did you travel to Vukovar, and why?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I travelled to Vukovar on business, and under instructions of the President of the Municipality of Kladovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you look at these documents and explain what they say?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The documents are in the Serbian and English languages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D69 and D69A.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please take a look at this, the part in the Serbian language, and explain what it is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order which proves that I went on business that day to Vukovar. I don't know what the situation is in the West, but when you travel on business in our country, when you get this kind of order, it shows that it's a business trip, not a personal -- private trip. It was the date, the 20th of November, 1991, we left in the morning, sometime in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why did you go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Because the delegation of the Municipal Assembly of Kladovo went to visit the reservists who were in the area of Vukovar, in its vicinity, and I was coming Mr. Nebojsa Lazarevic who was President of the Municipality on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you travel together?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not travel together. The gentleman in question had left earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your permission, I have only one copy of a big map of Yugoslavia, and I'm going to give it to you, but the northern part of that map has been photocopied. This is very big, as you can see. This is for all the parties.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map is marked D70.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could the usher please put the small map on the ELMO, and Mr. Jevtovic, could you show the town that you're from, the town you left, which route you took, and what time did you arrive. Could you take a pencil or something. Could you mark it? You will be pointing this out on the small map that will be put on the ELMO, so they will put it there, and please speak in the microphone so everyone can hear you. I know it's a bit difficult but ... Could you please show the place that you left, Kladovo, and how you arrived and which way you went, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I left Kladovo and I took the road along the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please show us the way you went?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Kladovo -- just a minute, please. By Golubac, Gradista, Pozarevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: And then we got out the highway to Belgrade. In Belgrade, in front of the Slavija Hotel, I picked up Mr. Tomasevic from Prijepolje and we continued to Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you take the same car?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the gentleman and I went together. Let me just find this. Backa Palanka, Novi Sad and Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't drive further than that. My car stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, I can't really show you the rest of the way because it was the first time I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you arrived in Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you arrive, approximately, in Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Around eight o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Around eight o'clock. The Defence would like this big map to be admitted into evidence as D70?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have a video camera on you, some kind of video camera?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I had a small radio cassette player and a video camera, yes. Just like any journalist. I always have this, I always use this kind of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you made a videotape, you filmed a videotape, and you brought it back home?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you gave it to Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could we please play this tape, D2, in its entirety, and with the permission of the Court, I would like Mr. Jevtovic to comment on the tape because he is the author of the tape, so if he could say where this is and when, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, you are going to say what is the town in question, what are the people you recognise, the faces, when you start viewing the tape?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this is the first moment when we arrived in Backa Palanka. This is about 8.37. This is in front of the -- this is Boris Vaksic, a journalist, Mr. Mikoracic (phoen), the Director of the elementary school in Kladovo. All of them are witnesses. Rado Matic who is a driver, and this is also a journalist from Prijepolje. This is a town that I first came to, so I am simply filming the panorama of the town itself, I am showing the municipal assembly building and other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And these dates, I mean, are they filmed --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are filmed automatically as soon as it is being filmed. The camera does this automatically, the 20th of November. We are indoors now, and these are things that belong to Croat soldiers, I think, and this was my first encounter with the war so I found all of this interesting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what this is. It's the first time I saw this and I found it interesting. I think they were sending this to their mothers, these soldiers, I don't know, they were killed perhaps. Mr. Ljuba Novakovic, the President of the Municipal Assembly of Backa Palanka. I interviewed him that morning. Djitica Milivojevic, and I don't know the other gentleman. Visa Maletic, the Prosecutor [sic], our driver, Mr. Nebojsa Lazarevic, President of the Municipal Assembly. Mr. Valsimic (phoen), he was an MP in the Republic of Serbia from Kladovo; I already mentioned these gentlemen before; and the driver, Dusan Iculovic. I don't know who this gentleman is. This is an office that we are sitting in. We are waiting for everyone to arrive so we could then move into the war zone. The gentleman was telling us about the consequences of the war. He said it was terrible that there were a lot of shells that had fallen, it was very interesting to me because it was the first time I ever saw the area. Mr. Dimitri Imolic (phoen), he's a new person here. Mr. Aleksic, I think he was an MP at that time in the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Jova Cvetkovic, a captain from Jagodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could I ask you, please, Mr. Technician -- could you please stop the tape so that I could put a question? After ten o'clock, new people arrived. Who are these new people who came in then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic and with him, Mr. Rade Leskovac and Captain Cvetkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Jovan?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: This is Mr. Letcovic (phoen), you can see him, these are persons I already mentioned, there is no need for me to mention them again, I think. I don't know this person either. A lot of other people were coming in. I mean, people from the government in Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You just tell us the names of the people you know, especially those who will be witnesses.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubo Novakovic, I don't think there is any need for me to repeat that. I already mentioned him. My microphone I used for interviewing people, Mr. Dokmanovic; my colleague, Boris Vaksic, interviewing Mr. Aleksic. This is in front of the office where we were waiting. This is still Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is Backa Palanka, this is the hall in front of the president's office. This is in front of the Municipal Assembly of Backa Palanka, we are waiting before we leave, so is the delegation of the Municipality of Kladovo, the people I already mentioned, and Mr. Dokmanovic is here too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (No translation)

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, this is another man. Off we go. This is 12 minutes past 12. We are crossing some kind of bridge now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please stop it once again? Did any people stay behind? I mean, any of the witnesses, the people that you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. We split into two groups at that point because we heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you please stop the tape because I can't comment on it and talk. Okay, it's stopped now.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: We split into two groups. We heard that you could not go through Vukovar and one group with Mr. Lazarevic, and I was in that group, and Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic, Jovan Cvetkovic, and Mr. Leskovac. We set out to see whether we could go through Vukovar, and this other group of people, the people I mentioned, went to deliver humanitarian aid to the reservists so we took that too as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This other group that did not accompany you to Vukovar, who are these people? Give us their names.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Frankly, I'm trying to remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But they're there, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Boris Vaksic, my colleague, then the team that took the truck, Djutica Milivojevic, Dusan Nitsulovic (phoen), then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, sorry to interrupt, but just the names of the people who were with you at the Atlantic Hotel?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Ah, I see. The people who are here now. Dusan Nitsulovic (phoen), Djutica Milivojevic, Boris Vaksic and Visa Maletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be it. Your Honour, with your permission, those are the four witnesses that are needed for two hours, only from ten to twelve in Backa Palanka, those are the two hours I am talking about, the ones that we mentioned this morning. Please continue with the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please continue your comments.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: We are moving towards Vukovar again, it's the first time I'm in the area, so I can't remember the exact names of every part of town, it was a long time ago. I know we stopped here and that I took a few pictures, I remember this through the window, and now we will continue on our vehicle to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What vehicle? This was Captain Cvetkovic's vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: It was a military vehicle. That's what we took. He drove it and Mr. Dokmanovic was in the vehicle, Mr. Lazarevic and I, and Rade Leskovac joined us, I think it was now that he joined us. This was when we arrived into VELEPROMET. I think that's the area we're in now. We parked the car here and we stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you can see the time on the camera, on the film. This is Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I imagine that this is the entrance into Vukovar. I'm not familiar with the area, as I said, but it's called VELEPROMET, I think, and I was filming this because we were waiting there for a certain period of time, so I talked to these people a lot. These people who were there, Croats and Serbs, who were in captivity. And with the people you can see here on this film. I talked to them as much as possible because I wanted radio interviews. This is Mr. Dokmanovic. I think that's him. Some of them knew each other. Everything happened in front of this building, in front of this building. This is a gate. It's practically a closed gate so that it's impossible to come in and out. So you can see that I could film this part, this area, it was a large area. This is the area that I'm talking about. There were a lot of women, people, children. I would go up to them, we talked freely. There were Croats and Serbs there, different people. It wasn't only one ethnic group. There were vans and trucks, some were parked in this courtyard area, some were outside in front of the courtyard. This was already around two o'clock. I remember they were eating some kind of salami, they were distributing them to all the people there. They received some food, some kind of aid, so we talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where was Slavko Dokmanovic at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I was filming at the time, so that I was following these people that were here. They were in the building, but they entered -- all of them entered the building. It was interesting for me to film the children with their mothers. That was interesting. Later, I saw an old lady, I remember I helped her to carry this enormous bag here. I felt sorry that she was carrying this enormous suitcase, so I helped her. I will stop now. I helped her to carry this bag. It was too big for her. Then I filmed these people. They were important to me to see how -- what their experience was, what a drama this was for them. I wanted to see their opinion, their thinking about what was happening in Vukovar. You see, I think these are nuns, they were eating these tins that I was talking about, they were issued by the army, and they were eating that before leaving on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you see any familiar faces? Just go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Only the people from Kladovo are familiar to me. These people, I don't know. This gentleman is a journalist from Piro (phoen). At the time there were some journalists there, at the time I don't know exactly which ones, I don't know if they were French, English, Dutch, I'm not sure. The guy from Piro translated into English. This is their camera, you can see by the camera. Mr. Hadzic is giving an interview. He would come out and give a couple of interviews during their meeting at that building, he came out several times to give interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did Mr. Dokmanovic come out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, at the beginning, when we just arrived, came in and out a couple of times. After that, he went into the premises. Later, I heard they had a meeting there, but he didn't come out during that meeting. At the beginning, before he came in and out a couple of times. After that, he went inside. Mr. Hadzic came out a couple of times. This is the moment when the buses are leaving with the women. I think there were men there also -- I think there were men on the trucks. These are buses. I can't exactly say how much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is this hospital staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I think these are international forces that accompanied them. I don't know which forces were in the hospital. I think these women are from the hospital. There were a lot of people, women, children, a lot of the population. They all came into the buses and the trucks. They were transported by military trucks. There was a long column. You can see the nuns here. He were they were in one of the trucks. There were a lot of the vehicles that they were evacuated in. It was offered for people who wanted to stay to stay and those who wanted to leave for Croatia could go. These are children. This is the moment when they were leaving the courtyard. There were a lot. I can't say exactly how many vehicles there were, but there were a lot. This is the gate, the courtyard, where we were. They are going out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just show us the familiar faces, name and last name. You don't have to be too long.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: There were men you can see who were evacuated, also women. Mr. Mirko Dragijic, you could see him for a moment, from Kladovo, a member of our delegation, he was there with us. This is -- I think it's a journalist, I heard later, it was a colleague, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What does it say on his --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Journalist, they told us where were we, why didn't you come earlier. We're scared you only come to film us now. They didn't like journalists much. They probably liked him but not us. I don't know. These are probably soldiers. I don't know who they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Only the ones that you know.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: This is in front of this facility, so we're still in that area. This is Mr. Leskovac, I think he was there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you're waiting all the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we're waiting to leave now. We're leaving about 15 hours and 16 minutes we're leaving, we're told we can go into the centre of the city to see how much of it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was in the car with you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Captain Cvetkovic was driving, Mr. Dokmanovic was in the car, me, Mr. Lazarevic, of course, and Gosperdi Radolaskovic (phoen). You could hear on the camera, we're talking during the drive, we're flabbergasted by what we see. It's extremely --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Whose voice could you hear?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I think I could hear Mr. Dokmanovic for a minute. You can hear Leskovac, this is Slavko Dokmanovic now, you can hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Whenever you hear his voice, tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I hear it now. I hear it now. I can tell his voice apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So just let us know.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: You could hear him now when he says, also now Mr. Dokmanovic is speaking. He's explaining to us. I'm in Vukovar for the first time and he's explaining to us where everything was, what it used to look like, what it looks like now. Both Serb and Croat houses were destroyed. There are no exceptions. Mr. Dokmanovic says the world has seen nothing like this yet. We were all flabbergasted by what we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please, every time you hear Mr. Dokmanovic's voice, tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: This is the part that we entered. I don't know exactly what it's called. This is the first time that I saw dead people. We didn't -- we weren't able to see dead people before. We were far from the front. This is the first time that I've seen these horrible things. Several people were dead there in the centre. I think there were two or three people there. The camera was zooming, but there were two or three people dead in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where are you now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: It's the same area, the centre. I don't know what it's called. The centre of the town. This is where we got out. I don't know what it's called. That's where the bus station was. I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you hear the voices?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There's no comment necessary here. You can hear Mr. Dokmanovic. He is giving an interview to my colleague from Radio Prijepolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What's his name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Vukosav Tomasevic, he was filming for Radio Prijepolje. You can see Mr. Radkovic (phoen), and Rade Leskovac, you can see Lazarevic. This is Mr. Mirko Dragijic, you can see him in the background, probably ambulance vehicles that helped in the town. Mr. Lazarevic, he is the mayor of Kladovo, Slavko Dokmanovic is still giving an interview. You could hear his voice and you can see him on the tape. The people that he talked to probably knew exactly where we were, but you could see by the bus stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But this is in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's the centre of the city, but I don't know the details, exactly what it's called. You could hear shots here. There was still fights in the town. I filmed this through a window because they said that the town was mined, so I filmed a house through the window. We were not allowed to go inside. These are some fighters who are saying that there is still fighting in the town and that we couldn't proceed because it wasn't safe. You could hear detonations, shots were still being fired. There was still shooting. I tried to zoom. I don't know what this is, some kind of facility, then they shot at us, so I took shelter because there was a danger. It wasn't safe. We were not guaranteed our safety. Now we're coming back from that part where we were. We're returning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Returning to where?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Vukovar. We were leaving from Vukovar towards Sidski Banovci, I don't know the locations of the streets. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Whose voice is this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: This is Mr. Dokmanovic. He is talking about the destruction of the city. The same team is in the car as before.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Whenever you hear Dokmanovic's voice --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can hear him now. You can hear him now, this is Mr. Dokmanovic's voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where were you going?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: We left Vukovar toward Sidski Banovci and you can see the time on the camera, and this is the time that he's talking about, 15.32, and you can follow our movements by the timing. This is when we came out of Vukovar, of that area. This is a looter and we were amazed that at moments like this, he was looting the abandoned homes. Slavko got angry there. He said this is such a shame for people. This is a park. I think there were a lot of trees and that whole part was destroyed. This is just professionally, it's a sunset, and I zoomed because the sky was so interesting. This is 15.42, that's the moment when we had to -- we caught up with a column that left VELEPROMET, so this is where we had to wait. They didn't let us overtake them. I was in a hurry. I'll explain later why I was in a hurry to pass, but they wouldn't let us cut the column in half, so we parked here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Stop the tape, please. This is the second tape. Yes, this is -- that's not the same tape. When you left Backa Topola, you passed in front of the municipality. Did you pass a bridge? Where?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: We crossed a bridge, I think it's called May 25th, but that bridge I remembered more because there was a checkpoint there, there was a checkpoint on -- before coming onto the bridge and before leaving the bridge. This was a military control so we couldn't pass. This is where we searched, if we have weapons, who are we, they looked at the truck with the aid, they wanted to see what was inside. After that, they let us go. I think it's called May 25th, but as far as geographical names, I don't know, so I don't want to make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said around ten o'clock Slavko Dokmanovic came to Backa Palanka. Do you know Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is he here? Do you see him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him when I came in and I see him now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Point him out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: That's him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I think at the end of 1990, he came to Kladovo on his trips for the first time. He cooperated as the mayor of Vukovar with our mayor of Kladovo, Nebojsa Lazarevic, and he visited at the beginning of 1991, there were different meetings where they talked about aid to Vukovar, probably some possible cooperation later when he wasn't no longer the mayor, he came less, but he did come to Mr. Lazarevic wedding, I think that was the end of September, in 1991. I think he was at Mr. Lazarevic's wedding for two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you tell us what kind of a man he was? Was he aggressive, quiet?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no. We had the opportunity to sit at the wedding and a couple of times after these official delegations, the journalists would be invited to dinner. He was a quiet man. I can only say the best about him. I was not at his level personally to spend time with him. We only had some contacts, but he was extremely peaceful and correct person. He's an ordinary man, like any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you left Vukovar on the way back, is the same team in the car as the one that came in?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: When we left the centre to go back, yes, it was the same group of people in the Lada all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Say who it was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Captain Cvetkovic was driving, Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Dokmanovic, Mr. Leskovac and myself were in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So all this time you sat together?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did you record with your video camera? Were you ordered to record Slavko Dokmanovic or something else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, not Mr. Dokmanovic. My goal was to follow the mayor, Mr. Lazarevic, so I recorded those activities which were interesting because I have to say the camera that I used to record is an amateur camera, it's not a professional camera, it's a small Japanese camera, JVC, it has a 30-minute tape so I couldn't tape all day. Secondly, I couldn't know what this tape would be used for. Today, I had a tape for Mr. Lazarevic so that he would have a remembrance of where he was in order to kind of justify this aid, because the municipality of Kladovo wanted us to tour that area, they wanted a picture of a -- realistic picture of what was going on and what the situation was there. So my goal was not Mr. Dokmanovic, my goal was Mr. Lazarevic. And Mr. Dokmanovic, I filmed incidentally when he was close by. You could see that from the tape. If I had known this would have been important one day for Mr. Dokmanovic, I probably would have taped more, but who knows?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't hear the question from Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The original tape, it's a small tape, it's impossible to watch unless you have an adapter, professionals know this, so it is an amateur camera with small tapes. I had to transfer it to a videotape. I copied it in two copies. I gave them to Mr. Lazarevic, the small tape I copied later. Mr. Lazarevic has both copies. I didn't take a copy, I gave them to Mr. Lazarevic. He's my neighbour, close to me. I could take it whenever we needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, the tape we saw now, is that exactly the same as November 20th when it was filmed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. It was the original tape. There are no changes. No, there are no changes, no cuts. If a professional is viewing this tape, I am an amateur, I'm not a TV camera man. The camera goes from one object to the next very quickly. I was more interested in recording these moments. It's a part of history. I didn't do this professionally, and you could see that this is not professional work because the tape was only 30 minutes long, I had to save the tape. So much sometimes I would tape. I also made ten radio interviews with my tape recorder that day so that there are time gaps there, but I can tell you that the timing goes on automatically so it's impossible to edit, and I state with all authority that this is the original tape, unedited, and everything that was taped there is on that tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why did you stop taping? What time did you stop taping?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: You could see at one moment on the tape that it was dusk, that it was sunset, so it was around then. So it's an amateur camera. There are no lights. You couldn't film later. I used the last moments of light to record. After that, the camera would not tape anything in the dark, so this is the only reason I didn't film any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you left Vukovar, you said you stopped somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: This is the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You can see the buses. Is that the first inhabited place that you came across?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was very close to Vukovar, I don't know how close. We caught up with the column of the buses. They were lined up, the entire column was lined up. We overpassed the column, and if you allow me, Your Honours, to explain -- I had a death in my family, so I had to cross the bridge by 7 p.m. in order to get back to Backa Palanka territory in order to go to Uzice, my uncle was dead, the funeral was the next day, so I had to rush, so this is the reason we hurried, to overtake the column in order to cross the bridge before 7 because the curfew went on then and we couldn't move. Then we tried to overpass the column but they wouldn't let us. When we got there, there was military police, they said. Wait, these people have priority. So we had to wait for five, six minutes, I don't know exactly. After that, I used the opportunity to come out with my camera and record the buses. Mr. Dokmanovic tried to intervene, but he didn't have any authority with the army. They didn't allow him. Both him and Rade Leskovac said that we came as guests from Serbia, so they wouldn't let us overtake the column, so we had to wait. This is where we lost maybe five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When was the next time you were stopped?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: We travelled -- I don't know exactly what that place is called, but later I heard them say it was Orolik. Why did I remember that place? Because that was the most dangerous moment for me that day. Simply we were hurrying to leave the territory as soon as possible so I could make -- make it to the bus in order to get to the funeral and then in front of us, we came up against the -- an army, I think it was both the police and the army, they were quite drunk and aggressive. Simply that day, nobody was safe unless they were in uniform that day. The soldiers did not let us pass, and Mr. Leskovac came out to explain who we were and we were in a hurry, and Mr. Dokmanovic came out and he asked them to let us pass. A soldier, especially one soldier, was very aggressive. He wanted to fire at us. His finger was on the trigger, and if Captain Cvetkovic had not come out, he was in uniform with his ranks, and if he hadn't come out, who knows what would have happened. I have to be honest at that moment I was afraid because there was a danger that they would shoot at us, so I remember that detail, we got away then, I think it was about 5 p.m., 5.15, about 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How do you know what time it was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I was in a hurry, I had a death, and I was rushing to make it, so I looked at my watch a lot. I was hurrying, because if I didn't get to the bridge by seven, I wouldn't be able to cross it and I would not make it to the funeral, but this is my father's brother, and since I don't have a father, it was very important at least one of us to get to the funeral.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Translator didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where was your next stop. Where was the next place you stopped?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: After that, I think we got to Sidski Banovci. This is where I left the car immediately, they gave me a military driver and a vehicle to go to Backa Palanka and later to Novi Sad because I wanted to get to the funeral that I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: So this was about six -- 5.30 and 6.00, I don't remember exactly. A lot of time has passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where in Sidski Banovci? Do you know what he was wearing? You saw the tape.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that if it hadn't been for the tape, I wouldn't have remembered a lot of the details, a lot of time passed, and based on this recording, I remembered a lot. He had a waist coat. He often used to come in a waist coat when he came to Kladovo, that's what I remembered him by. I think it was some kind of hunting, it wasn't a military waist coat, it was a hunter's waist coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that you left Sidski Banovci. How far did you go with the military vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Up to Backa Palanka and then Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what these documents are that we are showing you?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be marked D71.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: These documents are photocopies of bus tickets that I used on that day at that -- it's proof that I travelled that day, that even, on the 20th of October at 19.50 by bus to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you look at this now, please? That same evening, you were going to Backa Palanka and then Novi Sad, and then Novi Sad-Belgrade, and then from Belgrade to Uzice. What is this now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: This is a copy of a bus ticket, Belgrade- Kladovo, the next day after the funeral, so after I finished my personal family affairs in Uzice, when I was at the funeral, I came back by train to Belgrade, and from Belgrade I returned to Kladovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The date is the 21st of October, the next day, and I would like to explain -- November, I'm sorry. I explained to Your Honour that it is usual to us, when we are talking about our per diem, I travelled to Uzice privately so I don't have the tickets from Belgrade to Uzice, but I have photocopies, the originals are official documents, so it's impossible to do anything else. The original documents are proof that I was where I said I was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The originals I gave to the registrar, and I would like these documents to be admitted into evidence, that the gentleman travelled to Belgrade on the 20th and from Belgrade on the 21st, these are original tickets.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I suggest that they be admitted into evidence as Defence exhibits D -- what number?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And their version in the English language or the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, who did you travel with from Kladovo to Backa Palanka on the morning of the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: With Mr. Mirko Dragisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And approximately what time did you arrive in Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately around eight. Possibly at eight, but around eight at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you have a translation of what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We now have the French translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You have indicated the purpose of the group going from Kladovo was to visit the reservists who were there in Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And these reservists, these were Territorial Defence soldiers who had been mobilised from Kladovo to go and fight in Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I can't really discuss military matters. These were reservists within the army of Yugoslavia, if you know what I mean. I don't know what the situation is like in your country, but all of us, up to the age of 60, are potential conscripts, you know, when the army gives us call-up papers, we have to respond and we have to go there, so there was a group from Kladovo there who acted within the Yugoslav army, so they were reservists within the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But they had been mobilised to go and fight in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were fighting in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Is Vukovar in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: At the point when the war was breaking out, Vukovar was a Yugoslav town, and the Yugoslav army was defending one of the Yugoslav towns, Vukovar, because in 1991, Yugoslav was still there, in those borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, in the Socialist Federalist Republic of Yugoslavia, there were six republics, were there not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: And two provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And one of those six republics was the Republic of Croatia, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And is Vukovar on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, be it in the SFRY or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: If I would be going into somebody else's territory, I would have been asked to show a passport. Nobody ever asked me for a passport. I even went to school in Zagreb, and I never needed a passport to travel there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, the question is very simple: Is Vukovar in the Republic of Croatia, "Yes" or "No," and then you can explain if you need to.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Vukovar is a town within the Republic of Croatia but within the State of Yugoslavia. The State was called Yugoslavia then and the republics were constituent elements of that state.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after you went to Backa Palanka, what route did you take from there to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I told the gentleman who was questioning me in Belgrade too that I can't really recall all of the details related to that trip. It was the first time I took that route. I remember we crossed a bridge or something. But I can say that I cannot remember the actual topography, the toponyms, because I had never been there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who exactly was in the vehicle with you, going from Backa Palanka to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, of course, then Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic, and Captain Jovan Cvetkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who was driving the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Captain Jovan Cvetkovic, it was his vehicle, it was a military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was his assignment within the military, this Captain Cvetkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not qualified to answer that question. I'm not a military man myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where was he based at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I first met the gentleman in Backa Palanka at that meeting, so I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And to your knowledge was he active duty military or was he a reservist who had been mobilised?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I think he was a reservist. Before that, he was President of the Municipal Assembly of Jagodina, so there was no chance that he was an active military officer. He must have been a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And he had the rank of Captain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At the time was he still the President of the Municipality of Jagodina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long did it take you approximately to get from Backa Palanka to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: One travelled very slowly. There were military checkpoints every few kilometres. We were stopped by the military police, they would search our car. I think about an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were there any other vehicles travelling along with your group?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: With our group, when we left, Mr. Leskovac took his vehicle, but I think it broke down a bit after we crossed the bridge, so then he went into our car and then there was the car of the municipality of Kladovo, Mr. Dragijic was there, and the driver, Ivezic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So Mr. Leskovac got into your car between Backa Palanka and Vukovar; is that correct? Can you answer out loud, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I don't know exactly at which place this happened. We crossed the bridge. He had his own private car and I think his -- he had a flat tyre or something and then he went into our vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What did he do with his vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I think he left it there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that this was your first time in the Vukovar area, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: In that war zone, yes. I told you that I used to take my postgraduate courses in Zagreb, so I never really visited. Sometimes I travelled near that area, but these are small villages and towns, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And then you returned there again about a week later, on the 28th of November, when you made an additional film; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. After that, a delegation of our workers employed abroad, that wanted to help rebuild the city, came back and that's when I went again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And have you been to Vukovar again since that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think I went again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But based on your visit on the 20th and then again on the 28th, you were able to become somewhat familiar with the town. I know you don't know it in detail, but you have an idea about where some of these locations are; is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No. I only became familiar with the area that I actually visited then, not the other parts. It was very difficult to move around at that point. It was under strict military control, so you couldn't really travel elsewhere. You couldn't really move where you wanted to. Even journalists had restricted movement, so we couldn't really move around. To tell you the truth, once you've seen two or three of these streets, you've seen it all. I didn't really want to get very familiar with the details of the town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you recall what time you arrived at VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I think around two o'clock. If -- I must tell you one thing, quite frankly. If it weren't for the camera, I couldn't recall any of these details, after seven or eight years, or whatever. If I were to ask you what you were doing at this time seven years ago, you certainly couldn't remember, and if it weren't for the camera recording, I really couldn't remember. So I saw this on the film. I realise where I was. I also recall some of these other details. Otherwise, I really couldn't have remembered many of these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Have you ever been into a city that had been involved in a war before at this date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I assume that the impressions that it made on you were somewhat memorable?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Very grave, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at VELEPROMET, who was with you at that time? Was it the same people that had left Backa Palanka with the addition of Mr. Leskovac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what happened after you arrived at VELEPROMET? What occurred then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: We found a lot of people there. You could see it on the film, that there were a lot of people there. I took the camera so that I could record a bit of it because at the same time I was using my cassette recorder to record some interviews that I was making. I already told you I interviewed Serbs and Croats to see how they felt about the future and what the consequences would be and I talked to some of these elderly people. Simply, I was doing this along parallel lines. I was working for radio and also I was filming this. There were a lot of people there. There were a lot of people I didn't know there. I knew some of them from television, but I mostly knew the people who came in the same car with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you recognise Arkan on the videotape and on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you interview him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I knew the gentleman from television, from the newspapers, but I didn't know him personally. I didn't interview him. I only took his picture because some of these people wanted to have their pictures taken with him, and you can see that at one point in time when viewing the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you stay in the yard at VELEPROMET the entire time or did you go inside any of the buildings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't go into the building, not at a single point in time. I was in front of the building in the yard all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And approximately how long were you there altogether?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: If I were viewing the tape now, I could tell you exactly, but I think it was approximately an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know what your plans are for the schedule. Is this the time that you would prefer to take the break, or if so, I could continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. So we take 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: --- Resumed at 11.25 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, you have indicated that while you were at VELEPROMET, that some of the people were going in and out of the building. Were you aware of what type of meeting was taking place there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Much later, I heard that there was a meeting there of the government of SAO Krajina. That's what it was called. I knew a lot of people whom I had known the media only before that, but I didn't know anything about the meeting. I remember that there was a small prefabricated building there, they were going in and out of it, but I don't know what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, when you say that it was much later that you learned that this had been a meeting of the Serbian Autonomous District Government, was this later that day or was it sometime after that day that you learned of this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: A few days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: After the meeting concluded, was there any discussion as to what had taken place during the meeting by anyone who was there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. The people I was with had no contact with these other people. We were waiting for Mr. Dokmanovic, and we practically had no contact with anyone else. We were talking about the consequences of the war and what had happened, but what was going on in that small building, we had no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But Mr. Dokmanovic was a participant in this meeting, was he not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: He was indoors; I imagine that he took part in the meeting. I don't know who were the participants in the meeting, I don't know. But Mr. Dokmanovic was in the building all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And when he got back into the car, he didn't say anything to you about what had gone on in the meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No reason for him to tell me anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, at some point, your group left VELEPROMET. What brought this about? What was the purpose for leaving?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Our purpose, as we came there, was to see the town, to see the effects, to see how much had been destroyed, and since we were told that that part of the zone was safe now, we were told that we could have a look there. That was the only reason. We were supposed to see the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And with whom exactly did you leave VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The same as when we came there. I mean, as far as the vehicles are concerned. Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Dokmanovic, Jovan Cvetkovic was driving, Mr. Leskovac and I, in one vehicle, that is. And in the other vehicle, Mr. Dragisic, Colleague Tomasevic, and the driver, Ivezic. You can see it all on the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you left VELEPROMET, did you proceed directly to the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We drove slowly, but we went straight. We didn't stop anywhere. We had to move very slowly. You saw that there were a lot of ruins there and it was mentioned there were even mines there, so we had to drive very carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you filmed this interview which took place of Mr. Dokmanovic in the centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I filmed him, but Mr. Tomasevic interviewed him; my colleague, Mr. Tomasevic. I only filmed him, you know, with the camera, so it was only certain pictures that were taken in this way, but I only pictured them talking to one another during the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you film the entire interview or not; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly not. The interview went on for about ten minutes or so. I'm not too sure. I only had a few frames because I didn't have enough tape. I wanted to be as economical as possible with the tape. I told you it was a short tape, only 30 minutes, so I wanted to capture as many details as possible. They talked probably about ten minutes or so because, you know, a radio interview takes about ten minutes because people have to have something to say, so the camera is much shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you know why he chose to interview Mr. Dokmanovic as opposed to someone else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: You should ask Mr. Tomasevic that. But we were interviewing all the people that we could find there who had lived in Vukovar for years who are a part of Vukovar. Mr. Dokmanovic was a man who was in Vukovar for a long time, a man who was born in that town, and how he felt when he saw everything that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was Mr. Dokmanovic's reaction to what he saw that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: He was very sad and surprised. He didn't believe that that kind of thing was possible either. I think that it was his first time that he got into town then. I think he hadn't been in there before that, but he was horrified because he didn't realise that the city had been destroyed to such an extent and he was very sad about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that these are the reactions of everyone that was in your group?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We were all sad about it and surprised too, and we were also sorry that the town had been destroyed to such an extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And there was some anger also, was there not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. Not in our case, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Well, as you listened to the tape, there's some people cursing the Ustashe mothers of these people for what they have done. Do you recall conversations to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of people there, a lot of the military too. Probably there was a lot of disappointment on both sides, you know, because in a war, it was not only one side that was shooting but both sides were shooting and probably on both sides there were people who were shooting, who were destroying, and on the other hand, on both sides there were people who didn't want any shooting and destruction to go on either. So it wouldn't be fair to say that one side was horrified and the other side wasn't. I think that any honest man would have been horrified by what they had seen that day. Mr. Leskovac I think was cursing Ustashe mothers that day as we were watching all this. But I think this is the kind of revolt (sic) that you would also be expressing if you saw that kind of thing happen to your town, the town that you're from. So it's not some kind of hatred, you know, or hatred towards a particular nation or something, it is hatred towards destruction and towards those who did it because any one of us would feel sorry about that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But obviously the people who were cursing Ustashe mothers felt that the Croats were responsible for this destruction; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: You know what? When two men are fighting, then probably they are accusing each other of having hit each other. So one side was accusing the other side and this other side was accusing the first side, and that's the way these things usually go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, when you left the centre of town, who was with you in the car?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: You mean when we were leaving Vukovar, the centre of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That's correct, after this interview with Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was the same, Captain Cvetkovic was driving, then Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Dokmanovic, and Mr. Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: After you left the centre, where did you go exactly from that point on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: This road led out of Vukovar, so we were moving towards the place that we were supposed to reach, that is Sidski Banovci. And I'm not familiar with the names of all these places en route. But I know that we stopped after the first few kilometres, what I already mentioned when we met that group that had left town, the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: After leaving the centre of town, did you stop anywhere else in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. It was too dangerous to leave a vehicle. I mean, there was still shooting. I think that the city wasn't really safe even at that point, and we were in a hurry because I wanted to get back as soon as possible so that I could get to the funeral that I mentioned to you already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this point, I would like for the witness to be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit P4, if he could, please, which is the map of the Vukovar region, and this can perhaps be displayed on the ELMO. And if the technicians can also bring the tape up to the point where it shows the group leaving the centre of Vukovar? And we can start from that point. Just a moment. We need to move the map, I believe, a little bit. It's highlighting the part around Vinkovci. It needs to go more towards Vukovar. It still needs to come down some.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand what I was supposed to do. What am I supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Nothing at this point. I just want you to look at this map and I want to ask you a few questions. If you can, in looking at the map, does it refresh your memory a little bit in terms of the route in which you took?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, not really, no. I'm really not familiar with this. I'm not professionally familiar with maps, so perhaps it's easier for other people who are professionally involved. I know that this is Vukovar, but I'm not really familiar with all these other places. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well. You cannot read a map?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, and I wasn't even driving at that point, so I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you have indicated then -- well, we can take away this exhibit if the witness cannot read it. You indicated that you left the centre of town and that you headed directly out from Vukovar without making any further stops in the town of Vukovar; is that correct? If we can start the film now from the point where you're leaving the centre of the city? (Videotape played) I'm sorry, if we can go back some? To the point where you're leaving the centre of the city. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If we can stop it for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, this, that is being depicted here, is the road that goes up the hill from the centre of town; is that correct? In the direction back towards VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Please, do not ask me about the streets there. This was my first time. I'm not familiar with the area at all. I didn't know it back from the time of peace. I don't want to say anything I don't really know. I just want to tell you the truth about what I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well. If you would continue rolling the tape, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see the film. I can't see anything here. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you recall the location of this church in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No. I remember the church but not its location.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This is leaving Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think that we were leaving the city in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And this is -- if you can stop it there and go back to the ... You indicated that this was, as you're leaving the town, this is on the road toward Orolik?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, that's not what I said. I said that we left town and that we first stopped at a point a few kilometres out of town. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I understand that. Perhaps my question was not translated correctly. I'm asking: Was this the road that leads to Orolik? I'm not saying that Orolik was your next stop. I'm just asking if this is the road that goes from Vukovar to Orolik.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I imagine that that is the road leading to Sidski Banovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But you indicated that you stopped in Orolik on the way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: That was the second point at which we stopped because we stopped twice on that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I understand that. But, yes, is it correct that you stopped in Orolik?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We stopped in front of a ramp. I don't know what it was, but that's where we stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: As you leave Vukovar at this point and you were headed south in the direction of Orolik and Sidski Banovci, where was the next point that you stopped?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Please, let us be precise. Don't tell me south or north because I'm not an expert in geography and I don't know in what direction we were moving. We were moving toward Sidski Banovci. I don't know whether it's north or south or west or whatever. I mean, I want to tell you exactly what happened. I just know we were going there. So I remember that we stopped at Orolik because they were pointing guns at us and all that, but please don't ask me about this geography because I don't want to lie to you. I don't know. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to be as precise as I can, Mr. Jevtovic, and trying to get this as detailed as possible. As you are leaving Vukovar in the direction of Orolik and Sidski Banovci, where was the next point you stopped after this footage that we see here at 15.36 which you have testified is the southern end of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I didn't say that. Let us be quite accurate. I said that there was a place two or three kilometres away from Vukovar. I said that I couldn't speak of the south or west because I'm not familiar with that. I didn't say that at any point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I'm trying to be fair to a maximum, as long as we're not talking about north, south, east, and west. They're putting words in his mouth. This is not cross-examination; this is putting words into his mouth, something he never said. Can he read that? Where did he say at the southern end of town? If that is what Mr. Williamson is saying, can he read this out to us, tell us where he read this from?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Fila would read the question and the witness would read the question, I made no mention of direction in this question. I said, and I will repeat it: "I'm trying to be as precise as I can, Mr. Jevtovic, and trying to get this as detailed as possible. As you were leaving Vukovar, in the direction of Orolik and Sidski Banovci, where did you stop next?" I think that's fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But please do refrain from mentioning north or south because the witness made it clear that he has no sense of the directions. Simply mention their names --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That's why I did omit it in this question and then the reply was, "You're asking me directions again." I specifically omitted it, and then his response was that I was asking that. In the prior question, I had indicated that. I will ask this again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
