utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, after you left Vukovar at 15.36, the portion which is depicted on the videotape which you have testified as the end of Vukovar and you were headed in the direction of Orolik and Sidski Banovci, where did you stop next?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe the interpretation is not correct. I wasn't speaking about the route, I was talking about the going out. I said then that I don't know the toponyms, I don't know the names of the places because I wasn't in that area, whether the exit is in the north or the south, and I thank Your Honour for intervening. I do not wish to be brought into any confusion here. I wanted to say what happened so that we can let all the facts be known. We went out of the town two or three kilometres outside of the towns -- we stopped. There was a column of buses which we wanted to overtake. We were stopped by the police. They didn't let us overtake them until they passed. I don't know the name of that place. I know it's two or three kilometres away. We were going towards Sidski Banovci, the direction that we were moving, so that I could return and cross the bridge before seven o'clock. I think I was quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you do not know the name of this place where you stopped; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, I heard a lot of names, a lot of places, Tovarnik, Ernestinovo, Negoslavci. You know, this went through my ears. Would you know, if I brought you to my region for the first time and I gave you the names of 50 villages, would you remember them?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that it was the next inhabited village after you left Vukovar where you stopped, which I believe you testified in your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you aware that on this road between -- leaving Vukovar and this next village that there is a turnoff to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't turn anywhere, we went straight, went towards Sidski Banovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So it is your testimony that from the point you left the centre of town, that you continued travelling in the same direction without any alterations, any stops, or any turns until you reached this next village after Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm the father of two children and I have a Ph.D. in Political Sciences. When I decided to come here, I decided to speak only the truth, and I would like you to conduct yourself towards me accordingly. We were going towards Sidski Banovci, we didn't turn anywhere, and I described the road we were going in detail. And for what I'm saying, I guaranteed that that's what it was -- that's how it was and that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So I take it from what you are saying that my question was correct, that there were no turns, no stops, no alterations, and that you continued in the same direction from the time you left the centre of town until you stopped where we see these buses at 15.42 on the videotape. "Yes" or "No"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And who was with you in the vehicle during this time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: All the time, it was the same group. You already asked me. It's the same. I don't need to repeat that. If you want me to repeat that again: Mr. Cvetkovic, Mr. Dokmanovic, Mr. Leskovac, myself, and Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you didn't get out of the vehicle at any time until you made this stop where you filmed the buses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. When we got to the buses, that's -- Mr. Leskovac came out to try to intervene for them to let us go before the buses because I was in a hurry. I came out to film a few shots, but they didn't let us pass, so that we all came back -- military police was there and told us to get back into the vehicle, and when the buses passed them, we could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What type of camera did you use to make this video?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: It's a small camera, Japanese manufacturer, JVC. I think the gentleman who questioned me had the opportunity to see it. I brought it for him to see it. It's a camera that we usually use to film family birthdays, kids. It's a small camera of 500 to 600 marks. It's a small amateur camera. You had the opportunity to see it, and I could bring it back, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was this your camera?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the camera that I got from friends as a present.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And had you used this camera prior to 29th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I filmed often birthdays of my kids, a couple of times during Mr. Lazarevic's visits when various delegations visited, concerts attended by Mr. Lazarevic. I used it exclusively for our private use because Mr. Lazarevic and myself were good personal friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And I believe you've testified that this type of camera, the small camera, required a small cassette, a mini cassette, not the regular full-size cassettes that you would play in a VCR player?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And did you just have one mini cassette with you on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And the maximum time that you could record on this cassette was 30 minutes; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At what point during the day did you set the date and time display?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The time is automatic. I didn't set it. When I turn the camera on, the time comes on. So if I taped you now, it would be this time now that we are talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And there are numerous interruptions in the filming. When you interrupted filming, did you use the "Pause" button or the "Stop" button?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I turned the camera off. The breaks were out of the reasons I already explained. I worked with my radio tape recorder. So while I was talking -- having these conversations, the camera was turned off because I only had one battery. I had to turn it off. I wouldn't have -- the battery wouldn't have lasted if I was to record all day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you turned it back on, was it necessary to reset date and time, or was that automatic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Automatic. I already replied it's all automatic. The second that the camera is turned on, it shows the time and the place -- the time and the date, and it's always like that, even when I filmed the birthdays of my children. It's always like that. I have to tell you, it would be ridiculous to think that I then turned on the time and that this recording would be necessary after seven years. This is only just a matter of circumstance that it was kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At any point during the day did you rewind the tape to view something that you had filmed earlier or did you just let it run continuously?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No. Everything was recorded from once. There was no reason to rewind. I have already said it's not a professional film. Why would I rewind? Everything that was recorded was on that film. You see for yourselves that there are bad shots when the picture is shaky, the trees, the buildings were shaky, but I didn't take any of that out. I repeat, this is an authentic recording, and no interventions were done after it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And everything that you filmed is depicted on the tape that we've viewed in court today in the same exact order that you filmed it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I've already responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, when did you make a copy of this tape which has been introduced as Defence Exhibit 2? The video that we've seen today, when did you make that copy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: When I returned from Uzice, from the funeral, on the 22nd, I played my recordings on the radio, and then a day or so after that, I transferred the material to the big videotape and I gave it to Mr. Lazarevic. I didn't need it for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And the copy that we have viewed today in court, do you know if this is the same exact copy that you made at that time and gave to Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And did you use the same mini cassette to record the footage which was taken on the 28th of November when you returned to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: You think -- you mean that same tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The same mini cassette, yes, the small cassette.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: It's the same small camera. With the small camera, you use a small tape. If you think that same exact cassette, I'm not sure. I had a couple of them. It wasn't the only one that I had. I've already said that you can only film on that camera using that small tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could just view a little bit more of the videotape going back to this part at 15.36 again, just briefly? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This is as you're leaving Vukovar, and you indicated at this point that there is a sunset; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: You can see that on the recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well. And then this part, the next part at 15.42, if that can play, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: It's your testimony that this is in the next village where you had to stop for the buses; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: This is the recording with the buses. This is where I said we stopped for the first time and that the military police wouldn't let us pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what was the reason that you didn't film anything after that point?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said the camera is an amateur camera. I don't have lights, and you can see by yourself by the sun that it's the end of the day. There's no light. So that a couple of moments more I could record, and then after that, nothing more would be useable. If it was a professional camera with lights, I could record, but it was already getting dark so you couldn't really record any more. That's the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Only one thing that we need to clear up in order to have no difference. The witness Tomasevic, when the witness Jevtovic meets Tomasevic, he responded to my question but a little differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where did you meet Witness Tomasevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So he came into the car with you. Who else was in the car?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the three of you are going to Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Up until Backa Palanka in that car.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The three of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, I have a few questions. You may be of great assistance to the court if you answer my questions. First of all, you mentioned that there was in Backa Palanka around 8.30 in the morning on the 20th of November, there was a meeting, and we saw a few people sitting around a table. I wonder if you could tell us whether you were there -- taking your film, whether you can tell us what sort of topics were discussed in that meeting and why the three or four military people were present there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I have to explain first. I said that I came to Backa Palanka around 8.00, but the recording is from around 8.30. There was no meeting. This is where we gathered. We came from afar, I don't know, but probably from 300 to 250 kilometres away. Backa Palanka is the last municipality where there were no conflicts. It was a safe zone. We had to know where to proceed further so that that's where we were waiting. Mr. Lazarevic came earlier. This is where we waited for one another. We had to see whether our reservists were there. We didn't know where their positions were. So that was the only reason. There were no meetings. As you can see from the recording, there was no meeting. People are just sitting around. When we have a meeting, one person speaks and the rest listens. Here, there is nothing like that, it's just chatting. And at the same time, we carried out a number of interviews. As I said, we did an interview with Mr. Novakovic, the mayor of Backa Palanka, and other business people because Mr. Lazarevic established business, economic corporation, with Backa Palanka, so it wasn't a meeting, it was just gathering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I also ask you another question? I understand you were throughout with the President of the Assembly of Kladovo community, Mr. Lazarevic. He was with you the whole day. So what sort of clothes was he wearing: military or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, everybody from Kladovo wore civilian clothes, you can see that from the recording. There were civilians who came to visit our reservists. Not a single member of the delegation from Kladovo wore a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you, at some point this morning, you said that Arkan, when you were in VELEPROMET, Arkan came out of the meeting -- I'm quoting your words -- came out of the meeting many times to give interviews. Do you know what --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know whether -- or did you suppose that Arkan was attending a meeting, a cabinet meeting, a meeting of the government of the region?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I apologise. The colleagues who are interpreting; I'll have to check the interpretation. At no moment did I say that Arkan came in and out of the meeting. Mr. Arkan was outside, and you can see on the tape that he was outside. I didn't say that he was at a meeting. I only said that I knew him from TV and from the newspapers. I would need to check the translation later when we finish. I have the impression that the interpretation is not the most precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It may be that I'm wrong. I took down probably your words in a wrong way. Don't worry about that. In any case, you same that Arkan gave interviews while being there in the courtyard in VELEPROMET. Yes. One small question: I understand that the -- we saw that Mr. Dokmanovic gave an interview to Mr. Tomasevic. Do you know whether the tape is available of that interview?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: You have to ask Mr. Tomasevic. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. One final question: As a journalist, as an editor in chief of Radio Djerdap in Kladovo, were you not interested in what the cabinet meeting had discussed at VELEPROMET on your way back to Serbia, when you were to go to the funeral and so on? I wonder whether you asked questions to Mr. Dokmanovic about the gist of the discussions which had taken place at the meeting of government, of the government of the region.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to respond as I already responded. I didn't know on that day that there was a meeting being held there. In our country, the local media follow what is interesting to the local community. We don't conduct global policies. This is done by national media companies. For that day, for me, I went to follow the activities of Mr. Lazarevic. That was my goal. Not Mr. Hadzic, Arkan, or Mr. Dokmanovic interested me. I was reporting from the local aspect and following the events from the local level. So for me, it was important to state that Mr. Lazarevic was there, that he attended such and such a place, and I had no idea that there was a government meeting being held there. I noticed a lot of well-known people, but I didn't know the reason for their gathering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila, any question arising?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like to explain the misunderstanding. The witness said that morning that Mr. Hadzic came in and out several times and gave interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I may be wrong, yes. All right. Well, I assume there's no objection to the witness being released? No objection? Thank you so much for coming to give evidence in court, Mr. Jevtovic. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. (Witness stood down) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask you to kindly make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetkovic, did you give a statement to my office's investigator, Vasic (phoen)? Would you see if this is your signature, and do you acknowledge this statement as your own?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D73, English translation, D73A.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If there are no remarks from the Prosecution, I propose this be submitted as evidence, D73?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection from the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you finish law school in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you employed as a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I worked in an insurance company. Later I worked in a different company. I was the director of an insurance firm and then in another different company.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you become president of the Municipal Assembly in Jagodina?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Until June '92, from 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the meantime, you were a delegate of the Assembly of Serbia in 1990? Why were you no longer a delegate?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: My term of office expired and also for political reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You were in the area of the municipality of Vukovar on November 20th, 1991. Were you there before?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You had a captain's uniform with the insignia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a reserve captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you please tell us why you were there and why you had a uniform and the reserve captain insignia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I was the President of the Assembly of Svetozarevo, later of Jagodina. There was a large number of people there from my municipality; and in spite of the fact that I was against the war, I was there in order to try to help the people there who were in the region of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: They were there as reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: They were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, mobilised. I couldn't do anything else but be there and be with them unless I wore a uniform like all the other reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that's the reason you had the uniform of a captain of the reserve while you were in that region?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was there for under two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On the 20th of November, '91, did you see Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know this person from before?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I know him from 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is he in this courtroom, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he's over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did you meet him and why?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I met him as the President of the Assembly of Svetozarevo -- Jagodina, and he was the President of the Assembly of Vukovar, and because these two municipalities were sister municipalities, my first contacts were with him as early as '89 or maybe early '90, in the month of January. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, did you meet him -- were you with him on the 20th of November in Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I was there because I slept in his house. On the 19th I was there, I spent the night, I had dinner at his house, I slept in his house with a number of other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that a religious holiday, on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no religious holiday. He invited us to dinner. I don't remember. On the 21st, there is a religious holiday, not on the 20th. On the 21st, there is a holy day of Saint Archangel and it's an Orthodox Christian holiday and also an artillery fete of the JNA unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like you to watch a tape. Did you have this tape earlier? Did you receive this tape?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I received this tape from friends from Kladovo, from the President of the Municipality of Kladovo, who sent me the tape as a souvenir of the visit to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did he send it to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: He sent it to me the following year, at the beginning of '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like you to look at that tape that we will show you, and will you please let us know, when you see yourself, to tell us?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please play the tape. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please stop the tape.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I turned it off? I don't have anything on my screen. I probably turned something off.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at these photographs, and could you tell us whether you are on these photographs? At 10.38, if I'm not mistaken, is that you? A.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photo is marked D74.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where are you there and what time is it and what day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This was on the 20th at 10.38. This photograph is probably from the centre in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, no, no. Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, 10.38. At 10.38, I was in Backa Palanka. That's right, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now let's run the tape. Where are you now because the Prosecutor perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I am in Backa Palanka, in the office of the President of the Municipal Assembly of Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When Slavko Dokmanovic comes up, you show him to us, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: He's already been on the video film.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please run it again? Please show us Slavko Dokmanovic if you see him.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, here he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed. Please just say what is going on here while you're sitting in this room.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This was an informal gathering. We stopped in passing as we were going to Vukovar. We had set out from Trpinja and we were going to Vukovar and we were there in the office of the President of the Municipal Assembly. There was the President of the Municipal Assembly, Mr. Aleksic, who was an MP together with me in the Assembly of Serbia, and a couple of other people. I don't remember the names of all the people there. I was there, Slavko, Rade Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please show us to him when --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Here he is. Here's Aleksic in uniform. Then the man next to Aleksic was also an MP. This is the President of the Municipality of Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What's his name?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: His name was Novakovic. Yes, Novakovic was his last name. I don't know. I can't remember right now. I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you got that over with in Backa Palanka, where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: To Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: To Vukovar. How did you go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Military jeep. I drove it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What's it called?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Lada Niva, a red vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was in this vehicle? I mean from Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: From Backa Palanka to Sidski Banovci, to the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was driving --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic was in the vehicle. I was driving it and Rade Leskovac was with, the three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And Jevtovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Jevtovic was not with me then. Yes, sorry, no. Jevtovic was with me and the President of the Municipal Assembly of Kladovo. The two of them -- there were four of us in this vehicle when we set out from Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At some point in time, were you joined by --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Sidski Banovci, we were joined by Rade Leskovac. His car broke down somewhere, I don't know, somewhere along the road, and he joined us so there were five of us. Five of us in the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Five of you were in the car?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I was driving.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: From Sidski Banovci towards Vukovar, so there were five of us -- no, four of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. From Sidski Banovci, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't follow this, I'm afraid, it's going too fast, and I don't know what's --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is going too fast, really. I mean, I'll tell you. From Backa Palanka to Sidski Banovci, it was four of us. I, Slavko Dokmanovic, the President of the Municipality of Kladovo, and Zoran. He was director of the radio then in Kladovo. That is until Sidski Banovci. And then Sidski Banovci, when the car of Mr. Rade Leskovac broke down, then he joined us too. So five of us set out from Sidski Banovci to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you arrive in Vukovar in that composition?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, five of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And when did you arrive in VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: We arrived around 2 p.m. It's depicted on the tape. What I said to the Prosecutor was wrong. It was a slip of the tongue. We did not go to Vukovar first, we first went to VELEPROMET and then we went to Vukovar and you can see that clearly on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. From Backa Palanka to VELEPROMET, was Slavko Dokmanovic with you all the time in the car?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He didn't go out anywhere?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I would like to play a tape for you to see your arrival in VELEPROMET. Please play the tape. VELEPROMET, arriving in VELEPROMET and your stay in VELEPROMET. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And please show yourself. Say "This is me."

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is me. You can see me very well now, a bit to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is -- these are some women who were there, Croat women. They were there in the yard. This is a bed. I don't know where this was shot. I can't remember these people. This is Hadzic and this is Arkan and these are members of his escort. This is Arkan. His people from his escort. This is Hadzic, this is Slavko Dokmanovic in front of Hadzic. That's me. I don't know who the man kissing me is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please stop at this point.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see this man. I don't know who this man is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please, could you show these two groups of photographs to the witness so that he could say what's there? That can be a single Defence Exhibit, if you wish?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be marked as D75-1 and D75-2.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that's me. On the right-hand side is Goran Hadzic. I don't know the other men. And here behind me Lazarevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It's important that you're there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, that's me, on both pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please continue playing the tape.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is an acquaintance of mine, but I can't remember his name. The man who was saying hello to me, I don't know what his name is. I don't know anyone over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you in VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we're in VELEPROMET. This is me. I don't know these people. I mean, with the exception of the few people I mentioned, I don't know anyone else. These are the women who were getting ready to leave. Most of them were Croat women. These are buses and trucks that were to transport them to Croatia. These are some people, I don't know. These are the people who were getting ready to be transported. According to the information I received, there were about 1,000 women, primarily, and a few children, perhaps 1,500. This is an old lady, and I helped her before that with her suitcase. These are all the buses. The women getting ready to board the bus. This is a nun, as far as I can see. These are some of the local people of Serb background, I think, the workers there. This is Rade Leskovac. I don't know this man. Goran Hadzic. This is -- I don't know, I don't know. I don't know all these people. These are probably journalists. This is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please stop at this point. This is you at VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You had spent the previous night at Dokmanovic's?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was Dokmanovic wearing the previous day when you saw him, and that day, what was he wearing? What kind of clothes did he have on?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: He had some kind of combination, I don't know, some kind of camouflage uniform or a hunting suit, I don't know, some kind of combination. He was wearing a vest and some kind of a military coat, green, and underneath he had a waist coat and some kind of trousers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Since you were a reserve captain, was this some kind of regular JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't have any insignia, only the regular army had insignia. Many people wore different uniforms, but they didn't belong to the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What he was wearing, was this a lieutenant colonel of the JNA was it that kind of uniform, was it blue?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. He didn't have any kind of uniform. No insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was it blue, the colour of the sky?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was green and camouflage, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do airmen -- do members of the aviation of the Yugoslav army wear that kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they wear blue uniforms, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could I show you this uniform and ask you whether that is what Slavko Dokmanovic wore? Would you remember that? Can I show it to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can we show D48, is that what Slavko Dokmanovic wore that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I didn't get an answer from the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The answer to which question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But it wasn't translated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, it wasn't translated. Please, please put your question. What am I supposed to answer? That's it. I think that's it. I don't know exactly whether that is exactly that uniform, but this is what he wore, yes, yes. This is the hunting -- the hunting jacket he wore. You know, I go hunting too, and I have a similar vest. It's not camouflage like this one. Mine's of a different colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please lift it so we could all see it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please have a look. No, this is not a military uniform, and the Yugoslav army does not wear this kind of uniform, even army, camouflage uniforms are not like this. Yugoslav camouflage uniforms are different. It is light green and the design is different. It's bigger. This is some kind of imitation. This is really for huntsmen. You can see the pockets and also for the ammunition. So it's not for any kind of weapons. You see? It is for hunting weapons. It is for hunting weapons, for a shotgun. All right. And this, this, this is the colour of military camouflage uniforms. This colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the trousers?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, not the trousers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What do you mean "No"?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not military, that's what I'm saying. But this is the colour that military camouflage uniforms are, this one, like the shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would any of these three pieces belong to a lieutenant colonel of the Yugoslav army, of the aviation, rather? Even in the dark, would you say that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. First of all, the aviation, the air force, has clear insignia, and there is definite insignia showing that this is a lieutenant colonel and this could definitely not be the uniform of a lieutenant colonel of the Yugoslav army, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was Slavko Dokmanovic with you in the VELEPROMET compound throughout the period you were there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No. He was with me for ten or fifteen minutes when we arrived there and after that he went to attend a government meeting in a room which was next to us. We were standing in front of the entrance, and that is probably where the administration was of that enterprise. I mean, the offices of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could he have left without you seeing him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he couldn't have. There was that one single iron gate that we saw on the film and there is no other way of getting out so he couldn't have left without us seeing him. This is the way it is, you know. It runs parallel to the compound itself, so there is no way of getting out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So can I conclude that he could not have left the meeting throughout -- without you seeing him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he certainly could not have, and I was standing right in front of the entrance to that building and I did not move from there at all. Perhaps a metre or two, but not more than that so I couldn't have seen him, no. So I could see him if he would leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you saw the tape and you claim that he was in the building throughout this period of time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying, I don't know exactly where he was within the building but I think he was attending a session of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So where did you set out from VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I made a mistake there. I told the Prosecutor [sic] that first I went to Vukovar and then I went to VELEPROMET. No, no, it was a slip of the tongue. I was there first. So first when I came from Sidski Banovci and we came there. And later Slavko and I, this entire team, five of us, including Rade Leskovac, Jovan and Zoran, we went to take a look at Vukovar because I got into Vukovar immediately after the liberation. Vukovar fell on the 18th and on the 19th I was going to Erdut and I saw Vukovar and I told them about how terrible it looked so we went to see it and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you set out from VELEPROMET to the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we went to the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please stop at this point so we could run the tape and then you could show us your movement on the tape, so please let us play the tape. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I can see this -- well, I can only see houses. I don't know where this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please bring it back. We're running way too late. Please rewind the tape to 14.29 -- no, 15.05, for example. That's the time when they were leaving. Please, you're going to see the tape now and you're going to tell me who was in the car with you, what you're looking at. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What's this now?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: These are women that are being transported out of VELEPROMET. This is some kind of paramilitary participant. You see the insignia that he's wearing. They don't belong to the Yugoslav army. This is Arkan. This is Arkan again. This is Arkan. With a dog. I saw the dog too then. These are soldiers, obviously, on the APC or tank, I can't see well what it is. This is a reservist. This is a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's not important. Let's see when you get into town.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: These are members of the Territorial Defence, most probably. Buses, trucks preparing for transport, and now we are going down. There are houses that were destroyed, both left and right. This is a bit lower than Petrova Gora, that's where VELEPROMET is, this is below the barracks, there was terrible devastation there, the trees were destroyed there, the houses were destroyed. You can't really see this very well. I don't know where this is. So now we're going down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you hear the voice of Slavko Dokmanovic, please say "This is Slavko Dokmanovic's voice." When you hear Slavko's voice?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is Slavko, this was his voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Whenever you hear him, say "This is Slavko."

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Now we are moving down towards the centre of Vukovar. This is my voice. This is my voice. This is me. This is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When Slavko is speaking --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is Slavko, this is Slavko, this is me. This is someone from the back. Slavko is speaking about the Serb church that they destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just say "Slavko is speaking."

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is Slavko. This is Slavko. Because this was the first time that Slavko got into Vukovar. We stopped at that point someplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at these photographs. Is this where you stopped at twenty past three?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, may I ask you whether you have many other questions to ask the witness because --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What time are we supposed to break, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Half past twelve, but that's why I wonder whether you have many questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We do have more questions. I'm sorry, Your Honour, I thought that we were working until one o'clock. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Well, maybe -- let us ask these questions and then we will have a break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Documents are marked D76-1 and D76-2.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Over here in front by the right hand building, I stopped here. There was a corpse there and I didn't want to look at it. They went out to film it and I stayed in the jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please let everyone see the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: So on the right-hand side, from where you can see the car, we stopped 10 or 15 metres away from that, in front of this building there was a corpse, and they all went out to film it and I didn't want to watch that, so I stayed in the jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And this other photograph --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Ah, yes, yes, yes. This is where my jeep was and this is a bit further off. This is further off. I didn't even go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: These are photographs in that location?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's from my jeep and I was in my jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could all of this be admitted into evidence, and this would conclude my questioning before the break and then I would like to continue after the break, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. We will now take a break and we will start again at 2.00. --- Lunch break at 12.36 p.m. --- Resumed at 2.03 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetkovic, you saw on the tape the time printed when you left VELEPROMET to go to the city. Why did you leave at that time? What were you waiting for? What decided the time of departure?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Since Slavko was at the government meeting, we waited for him to finish so he could come with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that the reason why you claim that he couldn't have passed without you seeing him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I didn't see another different exit except for the main gate where we came in and where we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you look at these photographs now, and tell us which persons are shown on them and whose vehicle it is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D77.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just wait for the court to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetkovic, whose vehicle is it that can be seen?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is my vehicle that I was driving. It's a vehicle that I brought from Jagodina when I came to the front, and here beside me on the right is standing Rade Leskovac, the others I do not recognise. These were probably the boys who stopped with the car next to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who is the person in front of number 91?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: That is our -- from Prijepolje, journalist from Prijepolje. I can't remember his name right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You don't need to remember. Okay. That's the journalist from Prijepolje. Mr. Cvetkovic, from the time that you left from VELEPROMET, you told us who was sitting in the vehicle. You were driving. You come to the town, you left the town, so when is the first time that you stop after you left Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: The first time we stopped when we caught up with the column of cars, i.e. Transport vehicles, there were also trucks and buses that were transporting the women that we saw at VELEPROMET for Croatia, so the first time we stopped there, we couldn't overtake the column, we were stopped by the military and traffic police. That's where we stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just a moment. I would like to see the tape now which -- please continue the tape so that you can tell us where it ends and what it is? From 15.00 hours. There. Play it back a little more. Somewhere around the church. From there. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is still in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So what happens now?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: We're leaving Vukovar. We're going towards VELEPROMET. We're still in Vukovar. This is Slavko's voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who is speaking?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is Slavko's voice. This is also Slavko's voice. He said that the church in Dalj was like that. He says that all these were Ustashe houses. I asked him what it is -- he said it was a church, some kind of sacral monument of a Serbian landowner. This is an unknown person. This is also Slavko's voice. This was the park that was devastated. These trees were damaged. This is where the health centre was. This is the road towards Negoslavci. There were no vehicles in the beginning. There was a passenger later. We caught up with the column. These are the buses now. And somewhere here we couldn't go further. This is all Slavko's voice. We stopped here because the police didn't let us pass the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Stop the tape. So what happened then?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. We stood -- I don't know for how long, maybe 10, 15 minutes, maybe that long. We didn't leave the car at all. Then we proceeded towards Orolik, there we came to a gas station where there was a ramp and the soldiers probably stopped each vehicle. They stopped us. They mistreated us a little bit. They pointed their guns at us. Slavko went out, argued with them. I was at the wheel. I came out as well. They saw that I was a captain and then they let us pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was about the time then, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: It was almost completely dark by that time. I think it was after 5.00 p.m., around 5.00 p.m., I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you get to Sidski Banovci then?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: It lasted a while because there were cars, there was the column of cars, maybe slightly before 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. This is the question: From the time you left Vukovar and what we saw on the tape until your arrival to Sidski Banovci, who was in the vehicle that you were driving. Did vehicle change or was it the same group of people?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I think Zoran, the journalist from Kladovo, left earlier. I was in a hurry. I don't remember where he left the car, whether that was in Sidski Banovci or somewhere en route. I don't remember. But Slavko was with me all the time, Lazarevic, the President of the Municipality from Kladovo and Rade Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: From Vukovar through Negoslavci to Orolik, did you turn on the road anywhere?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't turn anywhere and we didn't stop anywhere except for those two places. We maybe were at a bend near Orolik, we waited a little bit because of a crowd and then we continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So can you claim that from the moment you left VELEPROMET to your arrival to Sidski Banovci, you didn't turn from the road maybe to Ovcara or whether Slavko Dokmanovic left the car?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. We never left that road, the road in the direction of Vukovar, Sidski Banovci, Orolik, except on those two occasions when we stopped in the column and when we were stopped by the -- at the ramp by the soldiers in front of Orolik and maybe if we stopped it would be for a couple of seconds to let some vehicles past.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So could you claim that Slavko Dokmanovic was with us all the time and you saw him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was with me all the time and he was sitting next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you arrive to Banovci?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Around 18 hours, maybe 18 hours, I can't specify.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When was the time you saw Slavko Dokmanovic for the last time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: We were there for an hour. We had a drink. We sat in a kitchen. It was a house which was the headquarters of the brigade, the command of the brigade. That's where I slept. We were there maybe for an hour, maybe a minute or so less, and then they left for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At that time it was dark?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was absolutely dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So when they left from Sidski Banovci, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: They left from Vukovar to -- I'm sorry, not Vukovar, for Trpinja, I apologise. Not for Vukovar, Trpinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We're finished with that. I would like to ask you something else. How long have you known Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I know Slavko Dokmanovic, as I said, from '89, as the President of the municipality of Vukovar. All the time I was in contact with him. I know him well. I know his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you describe him? Can you describe his family? What kind of a person is he?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I can say in just a few words that they are wonderful family. I know his wife, his daughter, his granddaughter, his brother. I visited their home several times. I know him as a quiet man, a fair man. Not aggressive in the least bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have political discussions with him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Before the war and during the war and ... I can say that he was not liked either by the Serbs or the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Because the Croats said that he was a state enemy because he had left Vukovar and because he lived in his village, Trpinja, and the Serbs objected because he did not organise the resistance movement in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you say he was a Chetnik, an extremist or something?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. He did not express any kind of nationalist behaviour. He was a normal person.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You were a member of parliament, you were a prominent member of the SPS the Socialist Party of Serbia. You talked to a lot of people, did you talk about Dokmanovic, what kind of a person he is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, I did not talk to political people in Serbia about Slavko Dokmanovic, but, for example, with the President of the Municipal Assembly of Backa Palanka with other people with whom I was in contact then. They all had an excellent opinion of Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it said SDS in the transcript, it is SPS, Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, but the transcript got it all wrong, it said SDS instead of SPS, the Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Finally, one more question: During all these meetings you had and these years of acquaintance, did you have any impression of your own, how his neighbourhood and his -- and the people around there regarded him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: He is from a well-known peasant's family, and he's an agronomist and he's a quiet man and he was not a loud person of any kind. I mean, he was simply probably elected President of the municipal assembly as an eminent citizen. At that time he was involved in agriculture. He was a member of the government because he was Minister of Agriculture, and he certainly was not Minister of the Interior or something like that. I mean, he was Minister of Agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have thus concluded my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetkovic, you were a President of a municipality in Jagodina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And your colleague, Mr. Dokmanovic, was, at a time, also President of a municipality; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And at that time, in the early 1990s, one had to be a prominent member of the community to have a position such as President of the Municipal Assembly, didn't one?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was a very responsible position?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, for that community that he lives in, I mean, where he is President of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean. And indeed one who attains such a position in the local community tends to be well-respected and well-known?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said that you had known Mr. Dokmanovic since 1989.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the end of 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you knew him to be well-known in the community?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I thought so because he could not have been elected President otherwise. People are supposed to know him. He was supposed to enjoy a good reputation because that is the only way in which he can be elected President of the municipality. It's not just anyone who can be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And he, like yourself, was able to exercise some influence in your own local community?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of the matters that were under his jurisdiction, specifically -- I mean, what do you have in mind, Sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Never mind. That's the answer I wanted. Now, during the period of the war in 1991, you had a military position, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was a reservist and I went voluntarily because many people from my municipality were at the front and I had a lot of trouble with their wives, their mothers, their relatives because people didn't want a war. You know that. You know that there were a lot of problems with mobilisation. So I went there so I would be near them, so that I could establish contact with their relatives, so I could give them things that they needed at the front, so I could send them supplies and things like that. So I was there as their support. And I did not have any military post except that I wore a uniform because I had to wear the uniform of a reservist at the front. It does not have any special insignia, it's the same like any other military uniform, but I'm a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Now, one of the reasons why you put on a uniform and went to the front was to set an example to the other people and members of your community that were there; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I was against the war, and that was not my intention. I didn't want them to follow me into the war. Nobody went with me or after me except for my driver who was there for a certain period of time. And -- he's a reservist too so he was there with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I wasn't really suggesting that you were, in a sense, leading your local people into the war. What I'm saying is that the people had to be there because that was required of them, and since they were there, you went there --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. They were not expected to be there, no. I cannot recall that any other President of the Municipality was at the front voluntarily except for me and that was the only reason why I was there. I don't think that a single municipality had so many people on the front as we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you didn't go there in any way to lend support or to give good example to the people that were there fighting? That wasn't your purpose?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I just wanted to lend my support to them. I mean, to have someone take care of them. They were reservists. There were very few active soldiers there. This was a brigade of reservists. These were people who were not very obedient. They did not really listen to their command, but they respected me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, who gave you the uniform to wear?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: The army, the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they give you any weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: But I didn't wear any weapons. I just had a revolver, my own. I did not wear an automatic rifle, I only had my revolver and a small Heckler.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you stationed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: In Sidski Banovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: That is 12 or 15 kilometres away from Sid on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, from a few kilometres away from Tovarnik and Ilaca on the road to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do there? What was your daily functions there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Every day I went to see the troops because they were deployed at various artillery points and I went to see them and food was coming in from Jagodina, cigarettes, and I distributed that. I mean, I accompanied these people who had brought it in and I distributed it equally to the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have a commander or were you just there of your own accord?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have a commander, I didn't have a commander, I wasn't responsible to anyone. No, I didn't have a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And no one was responsible to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No one was responsible to me. I behaved like a civilian except that I wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you visited the troops?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You moved around the front?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: The front was far away. This is 22 kilometres away from Vukovar. I was not in the immediate vicinity of Vukovar. There was the artillery brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you travel around?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I walked on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you get the vehicle from on the day you went to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: From the Electric Distributsia (phoen) of Jagodina, that is the power company in Jagodina. Since I did not have a jeep and the power company in Jagodina, rather the director of this company, they gave me a jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you require any passes or permission or permits to travel around the place where you were stationed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. The military authorities asked to see our IDs, there were checkpoints in Sidski Banovci, the military police always stopped us and they asked to see our IDs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what did your ID say you were? What position did they say you had?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Captain and the permits are usually signed by the commander, if we go to Sid or if we go to another place outside Sidski Banovci, then I have to get a piece of paper saying I'm so and so and I'm going to such and such a place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The commander in Sid wasn't your commander?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, he was not in Sid, he was in Sidski Banovci, and I slept together with them in the same house, I mean, but I was not under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. And --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: And I had to get permission from the military authorities because I could not pass if I didn't have permission of the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The place that you stayed in in Sidski Banovci, was that a place occupied by military personnel?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the meals, tell us about the conditions there, the food and facilities that were provided. Were they provided by the military?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: We got food from the military. We ate the same thing that the military ate, nothing else. We ate what the military ate too, so these are military cooks, and the cooking facilities were far away. We didn't really have a mess hall or anything, we ate there in the dining room of that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Along with the other soldiers that were there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Together with the active duty soldiers and the reservists, all the rest, I mean, who were stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. Now, this -- the place where you were stationed, Sidski Banovci, that, you say, wasn't near the front, it was a long way from the front.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Twenty-two kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did soldiers come back to this place who had been at the front or --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. This brigade was located there and it didn't move anywhere. It was located in Sidski Banovci, in Sid, and it did not move.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This brigade was made up of people that had come from your municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did these people that had come from your municipality, they had stayed there -- what? -- during the whole course of the war, had they?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you said a moment ago that you had a special gift in being able to control them because of your position back in your own municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not control them, I just wanted to make their position easier. I did not control them in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Didn't you say there were some that were unruly, or did I mishear that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that. They weren't very disciplined, you know, I mean, that's what I meant. They weren't like a regular army, they were like reservists. There were people who were older, there are people the age of 30 or 40, I mean, they're not real soldiers. You know what reservists are like. So they did not have the kind of strict discipline that the regular army had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They weren't part of Mr. Arkan's group, were they?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no way. No. I first saw Mr. Arkan there in Vukovar, when I saw him there. I didn't even know where he was or what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Dokmanovic during the course of the war other than at the time that you saw him in Vukovar on the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I came to see him before that too. I mean, I was with him on the 19th of November and before that. I went to see him at his village and in Erdut during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was he stationed in Erdut during the war when he wasn't in -- prior to him going to --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is where the seat of the government of the autonomous province of Krajina was. He didn't live there, but when meetings were held he was there because was a minister of the government. Erdut was the centre of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him there in his capacity as Minister during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what did you see him for? Was it official business or just on a personal basis?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: He would come officially -- he didn't wear a uniform except for the clothes we saw over here, and he didn't have any insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that. I was asking you when you saw him in Erdut. Did you see him in an official capacity or was it merely just a social, friendly meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no. Friendly. Friendly. I would even wait for the government session to be over and then I'd wait for him and then we'd go together to Trpinja or whatever. We were good friends. I was worried. And I brought beer from Jagodina and cans from Juhor to his village. I sent humanitarian aid to his village too and I took care of the people there and I was worried about them. That was the reason why I would see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Even so you are reserve captain during the course of the war, you still fulfilled your duties as President of the Municipality; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: While I was at the front, no. I had a deputy and I was in touch with him only over the phone and possibly I told him what to do, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Also, I asked him what he should send in for the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And -- but what I am saying is apart from your deputy stepping in and assisting you, you still officially maintained your position?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the day before you and Mr. Dokmanovic went to Vukovar, you spent the night in his house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, I spent the night at his house in Trpinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What time did you arrive there; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: It was dark. I think it was around 6.00 p.m., there was a football game, Vezna (phoen) was playing and I'm a fan and we wanted to watch the game and there was no electricity in Trpinja, so Rade Leskovac wanted to find a TV set and he stayed somewhere else and he didn't even come back and so we had to listen to the game on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was the decision made to go into Vukovar on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: That evening. I came there with that intention, I saw Vukovar on the 19th. He hadn't seen it before that. And the President of the Municipality of Kladovo, Lazarevic, and other people came and they all wanted to see it because I told them all about it, I told them how horrifying it was and they all wanted to see it because Vukovar had been liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you went there also, didn't you, to -- as a demonstration of support for the people of Vukovar and the region?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: What are you referring to? I mean, going to Vukovar or generally speaking about when I went there or are you talking about that specific day, the 20th? I don't really understand your question. It's not very specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go there just out of curiosity to see what had happened or did you go there because you were President of the Municipality and that you wanted to show the people that you supported them, those people that suffered as a consequence of the war?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: You are referring to people from Vukovar or are you referring to my people who were at the front? Could you please be more specific? I don't exactly know what you are referring to. Are you referring to the people from this region or are you referring to the reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, were your reservists at Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, obviously you didn't go there to support those people.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I went to Vukovar with the intention of going to Erdut, not knowing that I could not go through Vukovar. I found out on the 19th from the commander that Vukovar had been set free, had been liberated, but I could not go through Vukovar, and the military showed me the map, and I went back to Sidski Banovci and then I went there to Backa Palanka via Ilok to Erdut. That is to say I had not particularly set out to go to Vukovar, I mean it is much closer this way because Trpinja-Banovci is 40 kilometres, via Backa Palanka, Ilok, Sarengrad, et cetera, and via Bogojevo Bridge, that is 100 kilometres to Erdut, and further on to Trpinja. And that is why I had set out for Vukovar. I didn't know what it was like at all. I was astounded. I could not have imagined that it was destroyed to such an extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But hadn't you been there only a couple of days prior to this, to Vukovar itself?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I had never been to Vukovar before that. I mean, during the war. You could not get in. That is where the focal point of the conflict was. Nobody was allowed to get in there. I mean, only those who were literally in war there. So, on the 19th, it was the first time that I had got into Vukovar and I went back again on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we're at cross-purposes because I was talking about the day of the 20th was the second time that you went to Vukovar, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the day before, yes. So I was there on the 19th and the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Dokmanovic tell you why he wanted to go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: He said that he was supposed to have a government meeting in Vukovar and that that would be the first government meeting to be held in liberated Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he say why the government were going to meet in Vukovar on that day, the 20th?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. He didn't say. But I didn't ask him about it either. We didn't really discuss it. I didn't ask him about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you knew why he was going. My question is: Why did you go on that day, the 20th?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: He was with me in the same vehicle. He -- I drove him. He had no other vehicle to take. He was with me all the time in my vehicle because the other man's car had broken down because when this car is broken down, he had no other way of getting to Vukovar except by my vehicle, and I wanted to go and see it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was the other man?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: The other man I'm talking about is Rade Leskovac who is deputy Minister of Information in Krajina and the third person was Lazarevic, President of the Municipality of Kladovo, and the fourth one was Zoran, the director of radio Kladovo, Zoran Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was Rade Leskovac, the deputy Minister of Information, it was his car that broke down, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where did his car break down?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
