utterances.text: His car broke down, he was following our vehicle, and it broke down somewhere in Sidski Banovci or somewhere near that place, I can't remember exactly, and then he joined us in our vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That would have been after you left Trpinja?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: After we had left Trpinja, then we went to Backa Palanka, and then we went to Sidski Banovci, it was the four of us, and then the car of Rade Leskovac broke down and he joined us in my Lada Niva jeep as the fifth person there, it was a civilian car.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But Mr. Dokmanovic couldn't have made a decision to go with you because the vehicle that was owned by Rade Leskovac had broken down because he wouldn't have known the car was going to be broken down until he got halfway there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: But he was with me all the time. I told you Slavko Dokmanovic was not with Rade Leskovac but with me in my car from Trpinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, but the point I'm trying to make is that I asked you the question why Mr. Dokmanovic went with you and you told us it was because Rade Leskovac's car had broken down. That can't have been the reason why initially --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is simply not true. Let the Prosecutor show the transcript where he said that he went with his car because Rade Leskovac's car broke down. That is not true. And, please, don't try to confuse the witness, but say all that is in the statement --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I said this out loud that Rade Leskovac, somewhere around Sidski Banovci, his car broke down, and that's when he entered my vehicle (FEEDBACK) all the time from Trpinja via Backa Palanka to Sidski Banovci, Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic was with me and the three people I mentioned, the President of the Municipality of Kladovo and also Zoran Jevtovic, the journalist. I said this clearly when Rade Leskovac's car broke down, he entered our vehicle, so the five of us then went to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I might respond to Mr. Fila. He doesn't seem to be following the transcript very closely, Your Honours, because at page 111, line 11, the witness answered in the following way: "He was with me in the same vehicle. He -- I drove home. He had no other vehicle to take. He was with me all the time in my vehicle because the other man's car had broken down because when this car are broken down, he had no other way of getting to Vukovar except by my vehicle." And that's what I relied upon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Maybe -- can you ask again --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Maybe you would need to resolve this question with your interpreters. I have been following this closely and I know the geography. This is my country and I know the road that they took. You cannot go to Trpinja to Sid without going through Backa Palanka, and probably Mr. Niemann did not bother to look at the map. If he looked at the geographical map, he would understand that the questions he is asking have no sense, and I am following this procedure. This is my country. I have to follow it and I wish the court would coordinate. It would be much easier then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, I would not say that the question that Mr. Niemann is putting has no sense, but I would like to call upon Mr. Niemann to rephrase his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't need to pursue it any further, Your Honour. I think the point is made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the next morning, when you got up to go to Vukovar, what time did you get up?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I got up exactly at 6.30, had a shower and shaved, they were still asleep, and then around 7.00 they got up and we left. Maybe we all had breakfast there and then perhaps we left at around 8.00. I don't know at exactly what time we started out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the other people, Mr. Dokmanovic, was in the house. Was there anyone else in the house that morning that left in the vehicle to go or was it just you and him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Lazarevic was with me, the President of the Municipality of Vukovar -- I'm sorry, of Kladovo, and his driver who left, I think he left with somebody, maybe Zoran, I don't remember, maybe he drove Zoran, his driver was sleeping. We were sleeping on the floor in the living room since there wasn't enough room. The house was full from the people -- the house's inhabitants and us, the arrivals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Lazarevic and Mr. Dokmanovic, if you can remember, have a shower as well and breakfast and then leave with you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had a shower. I was the first to get up, I had a shower, I shaved, I didn't have the opportunity to have a shower in Sidski Banovci, so I used the opportunity to have a shower here. I was dirty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did you stop on the way from Trpinja to Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember if we stopped. I don't think that we stopped anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when you arrived at Backa Palanka, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Straight to the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the municipal assembly of Backa Palanka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, municipal assembly of Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who made the decision to go there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I had met earlier with Mr. Novakovic the President of the Municipal Assembly, all humanitarian aid went through Backa Palanka, all humanitarian aid for the army, for the population, across the Danube went through Backa Palanka, and Ljubo Novakovic was directly responsible for that help. I personally sent trucks there with cans and other necessary things for the army, and we stopped by to meet with him there. It was said that some other people would be there. This was an informal meeting, wasn't agreed upon. We stayed a little bit, maybe had some coffee or a drink, I don't remember everything exactly, and then we left for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, at this particular meeting you attended -- I will withdraw that. Did Mr. Dokmanovic have anything to say about going to this meeting in Backa Palanka? Did he -- did you consult him about it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It wasn't a meeting, we just stopped by at Ljubo Novakovic's, there was no agenda, nothing was specified, we just said we would stop by Ljubo Novakovic's in Backa Palanka. So it wasn't a meeting, it was a stopover for a talk and maybe for a glass of some drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And this is something that you had prearranged, it was not -- it had nothing to do with Mr. Dokmanovic, is my question?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: The only connection was that Slavko Dokmanovic was with us, there was nothing special, not a special connection or that he had a scheduled meeting with a certain subject to discuss or for -- with a certain task. Nothing happened. It was an informal meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: We talked about -- the topic was the fall of Vukovar, that was the most frequent topic, and what will happen if the war is over, what will happen in the reconstruction of Krajina, that the people had suffered a lot there. That's generally what was talked about, what we will all help. These were the topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about dealing with people who you believed to be responsible for the war in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, we didn't talk about that, the responsibility of some people for the war in Vukovar, we didn't discuss that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There was no discussion about setting up people's courts or anything of that nature to deal with persons responsible, that you heard, at least?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, there were some military personnel there.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: We discussed nothing on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There were military personnel --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: There were a few military people, there was a President of a Municipal Assembly in uniform from Vrsac, Aleksic, who was stationed in Ilok, and he came in another car up until Ilok, he was supposed to come to Vukovar, but we forgot to take him so he stayed in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were any of the participants in this meeting armed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I had a gun, Jovan probably had a gun, we were there with guns, I don't know who had guns, I did have a gun, and I know that the reservists had guns. For the others, I don't remember. To tell you the truth, I don't remember seeing who had arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why was it necessary to have a gun at a meeting like this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: We were moving in an area where there was war. A gun is for personal defence, it's a weapon that serves the purpose of personal defence. People carry that when there is no war, never mind when there is a war situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you were in no personal danger at Backa Palanka, were you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not logical for me to take my belt off and to take my gun off when I'm in uniform. In war time, this is a part of the uniform. A person is armed. He doesn't take that off unless military authorities demand that I come in somewhere without arms. Then I would give them. But it's not usual to take my belt off and to take my gun off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what time did you leave Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps around 1.00. I don't know exactly. It must be there on the recording. I watched the tape, but I don't remember. I saw the timer, but I don't remember. I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it a difficult or long trip going from Backa Palanka up to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't difficult. The road was free. It was a round about way. We went through Sarengrad, Ilok, Sid, Tovarnik, et cetera, up to Sidski Banovci, but it wasn't particularly difficult. There wasn't a lot of heavy traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And this is an area which is reasonably familiar to you, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the roads weren't very crowded, I think is your evidence, isn't it, at that hour of the morning or that time of the day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, no. Everything was over. The army was moving when there was -- during the battle for Vukovar. This was the second day. There were no movements by military units. Civilians didn't move very much in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at Vukovar, what did you do? Where did you go first?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I made a mistake when I made my statement to the Prosecutor, I said I went to Vukovar first, but it was a slip of the tongue. First of all, I turned right away and I saw that on the film. I turned -- we turned right away to the transport company, this is where we waited for Slavko, this is where we saw what I told you before, and then we left for Vukovar. This is all in Vukovar, but this is on the outskirts of Vukovar. So I was in Vukovar, but I didn't go to the centre of Vukovar but to the transport company. But I made a slip of the tongue when I gave my statement to the Prosecutor who took my statement in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Never mind about that. You went to the VELEPROMET premises first.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did you ...

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Slavko told me that there is a government meeting there. I didn't have any particular task. Slavko said to go to the government meeting, and that's where we waited for him, because of that, for him to finish that. I didn't attend the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do while he was attending the government meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I stood there and I talked to people. There were a few acquaintances that I know from Vukovar. They introduced me to Arkan, who I saw for the first time in my life then. I saw Hadzic, I know him from before. I talked to him. After that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You keep going.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: After that, while waiting, I talked with different people. There was a lot of people there. Some of them I knew, some of them I didn't know. I stayed with the people that I came with except for Slavko, who was at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you said you had a conversation with Arkan. What did you discuss with him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: With him, he was wounded, he was showing me the sub machine gun, how a sniper -- a small calibre injured him while he was holding the gun and it came out through his index finger of the left hand, that's what he was talking about, and he also showed me a knife that some woman called Martha killed an 11-year-old boy who was exchanged later for Serbian prisoners. That's what he was telling me about. He was telling me about a dog, he had a dog in the jeep, and so on. There was no particular conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he go into the meeting, the government meeting; did you see that or not? Whether or not he went into the government meeting at any stage?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that he left, I saw that he left, not right away, when they did -- maybe after a few minutes, but where he was, I don't know. He went into the same entrance where the Ministers went in, President Hadzic and others. But where he was, I don't know, because I didn't enter the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how long after you and Mr. Dokmanovic arrived did President Hadzic arrive?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Very quickly, maybe several minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did President Hadzic arrive with Mr. Arkan?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that the two of them came in together, but I assumed that they did -- that group of people, Arkan and some with them, I assume Hadzic too, came in at the same time. I didn't really see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, your evidence is that you actually didn't go into the building where the Ministers met?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And so you didn't see the interior of this building?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw the inside of the building later because I came on another occasion a few days later, but on that day, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is there just one entrance and exit to this building, or are there other doors?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any other. I think there is one entrance, there's a large hall, it's a one-floor building, it's a modest building. I think this building is -- abuts onto another yard and there's no exit on that side. If there is, I didn't see it. But if there was any other exit, it would be into the yard, so they would have to pass through the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, after the meeting had concluded, you met up again with Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: We were waiting for him to finish the meeting. That was the point. And to go and see Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when he came out of the meeting, what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. "Let's go." Maybe a couple of minutes later, we sat in -- we got into the jeep and went to the centre of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he said "Let's go," did he say where to go to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we agreed to go to the centre of Vukovar, to look at Vukovar. He wanted to see it. He had not been to Vukovar before. But it's understandable -- this is also Vukovar only we were in the outskirts of Vukovar, and this was a part that was not destroyed much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when he saw what was in Vukovar, was he disturbed by what he saw?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: He was very upset and shook up. He couldn't believe it. He couldn't comprehend that it was destroyed that much and you could hear his comment from the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he angry?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: He was angry that it had to be that way. Why did Vukovar have to be destroyed in that way? Because if you think of a mayor -- imagine a mayor who enters his city and see how destroyed it is. What was he going to do? He didn't know who destroyed that or how. He had no idea. I didn't know when I went to see it the first time that it was so horrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, if we can see the video clip starting from the point where we're in the middle of the town, if we could start at that point, please, the town of Vukovar, and heading out? I'll probably ask for the video to be stopped on a couple of occasions as we go through.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps it could just play for a minute because I do have a question, seeing as we are here. Might the technicians move it forward for me, please? This is very early in the piece.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: After 15 hours, when the timer is at 15 hours, is that so? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you identified this earlier in your evidence as being at VELEPROMET; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is probably when the women were transported from VELEPROMET for Croatia on the route that I explained, and I said that this is a member of some units unknown to me. This was Arkan. Here it is. This is Arkan. And that's the dog that was in the car when he came. He was injured in his hand. This is some military vehicle, either a transporter or a tank, this is a reservist. These are all reservists. These are -- this is soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I don't need to be here. If we can move it forward further into the centre of the town. It's just leaving the town, at the point where we're leaving the town, the centre of the town. 15.26, I believe. I think this is in the centre of the town, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I still don't see if this is the centre. I don't remember seeing or encountering these vehicles. These are military medical vehicles. I don't remember. This is Nebojsa Lazarevic, this is a military jeep, this is Slavko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I don't want to confuse you, Sir. You just look at it and tell me if you can identify what you're seeing.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is Slavko here and "Korea", we call him "Korea" he's a journalist from Prijepolje, I can't remember his name -- last name at the moment, I just know his nickname, "Korea".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I don't want you to necessarily tell me who they are, just identify the spot, if you can. If you can tell me where it is, so just keep looking until --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Not able here. I don't see -- I only see a part of the building, I have to see the street in order to be able to say where we are. These buildings are such that I can't identify them, particularly because I don't really know. These are reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So this may not be part of Vukovar, it may be some other town?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no -- yes, this is Vukovar, these are the houses. This is down towards the centre. Here, these are the dead -- I saw one dead person. This is where already going down towards the centre. This is that church, the Orthodox church, that was destroyed, and now this, I can identify this -- this is the street that leads down to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is this going down into Vukovar or out of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes -- no, towards Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just stop for a moment. Stop the tape for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Down towards Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So this is the decent into Vukovar down from VELEPROMET, not the other way around; you're sure about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, this is a part of the street. I would be very imprecise about this. I would have to see more. I would like to show him --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown a longer segment.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Show me the part we stopped with the car and I will tell you what it is because I can't identify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please, would you show the tape to the witness from the moment they leave VELEPROMET, go towards Vukovar, and are coming back, but not to take it out of context and say this is Vukovar. Even Slavko, who knows Vukovar very well, cannot say what this is, and I can't definitely. Exit from VELEPROMET is at 15 hours and 17 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please comply with the request of the Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Mr. Fila is suggesting I'm trying to confuse the witness, which is the last thing I'm trying to do, then I'll start the tape right from the very beginning and go through it. I was trying to save the court time. The suggestion is that I am deliberately trying to confuse the witness, so would the technician please play the whole tape?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That's not necessary. Just the little bit. When you're in the centre, the centre of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: From 15.17. I apologise, Your Honours, from 15 hours and 17 minutes. That's when they started out from VELEPROMET this last -- for two or three minutes. I don't ask for the whole tape of 25 minutes. But if you ask a person, is this Vukovar from one tape, then you are trying to do something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm not trying to do anything else, Your Honour. I'm trying to ask the witness to clarify the position. Perhaps the tape could be played from 15.17? If that might suit my friend? Could the tape just be held there for a moment, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you have any doubts about where it is or you want clarification, please say so. I'm not here in any way trying to confuse the issue. I want clarification. So, please, don't hesitate. Now, if you don't understand it, let us know.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can the tape now be played?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand very well. From.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: From 15.17, this is 15.19, from 15.17, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please go back to 15.17?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I asked for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There doesn't seem to be one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the voice of Slavko Dokmanovic. He is saying "Let's go down there."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I don't want you to tell me --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: He is saying "Let's go left, but I don't see anything yet."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Please, do not recite what's going on. I merely want you to tell me locations. That's the only thing I'm interested in is locations. When you see a location that you recognise --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is Vukovar. Okay. This is the descent, going down into the centre of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If there are other parts that you recognise, can you please say so when you see it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is where the sacral monument was of some Serbian land owner. I asked Slavko what that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are we leaving Vukovar or going out --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: We're going towards the centre, no, we're going towards the centre. And here we are. We stopped here on the right side next to this building. This is where we saw the killed man with his eyes gouged out. I didn't want to leave the car. I stayed. And they went out, all of them, except for me. They went out to tape it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did they say when they went out? Did they say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: They were depressed. They saw a few other corpses. Everybody was depressed. Everybody was having a hard time. You can see here with the cut throat, I've seen this now -- when I was watching the recording but I didn't leave the car to see that. You can see that where it happened at the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next part of the tape I want you to indicate, Witness --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: -- when you actually start to leave the centre of Vukovar. That's the part that I want you to tell me when you get to that point.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: We're here now. This is where I went out of the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where are you moving to now, Witness? Where is the vehicle being driven to now?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Turned around and went back the same way that we came, the same building that we passed by, now we're going back. The same church that we passed by going down, now we're coming back. And now we're going back up the hill. I don't know if this is the same footage that was shown for going down. I can't say exactly. It looks the same. Until I see it, I can't really say. This is the way out of Vukovar. This is the sacral monument, it's near an Orthodox grave yard, and now we're making our way up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did you stop anywhere along this route?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, we didn't stop anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Isn't your vehicle stopped here --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Now we're going out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Stop for a moment. Stop the tape for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. This is a park. Perhaps we had a look at the park. There was a clinic somewhere here near the park. Perhaps we stopped there. I can't tell precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you stop --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't go out anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you stop anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Not here. We stopped only when we got out of Vukovar, somewhere near Negoslavci, where we managed to pass the column, that is the first point at which we stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If we could continue rolling the tape, please? So you're moving again now; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did you stop again -- I'm sorry, I didn't mean the tape to stop -- did you stop again after this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is -- no, no. There was a clinic here, Slavko showed it to me. We didn't stop anywhere, no. The road was empty and we were getting out of Vukovar and we joined the column only at a later point and we didn't stop anywhere. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where is this point here? Can you tell me? Where is it? This particular spot.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the road leading out of Vukovar. These are the outskirts of Vukovar. This is the road towards Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These are the last houses as you move out of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: The last houses as you move out of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the tape continue to roll, please?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: We are now joining the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Stop there. Are you able to identify -- I'm asking you if you could identify this place. Where are you here?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't, I can't. I can't see anything here except for the bus. I can't say exactly where we are. This is the road from Vukovar to Negoslavci, and Negoslavci is approximately three or four kilometres away from Vukovar, so it is on that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'll now ask you, if you would -- well, play it through, please. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's enough. That's finished. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, if the witness might be shown Exhibit P4? And could it be placed on the overhead projector. And, Witness, I'd ask you with a marker, with a pointer, to point on the road where you left Vukovar on that day, the 20th, the part that we've just been looking at on the video, would you please mark on the -- not mark, but with a pointer, firstly point to Vukovar and then the road that you followed out of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, when you talk, you'll need to speak into the microphone; otherwise, you can't be heard.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Vukovar is over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, perhaps the camera might zoom in on that for us, if they would?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let me see what is the road that we had passed. I can't find Sidski Banovci -- oh, here it is, Tovarnik -- I have to find Sidski Banovci. Probably this road here. Just a minute. Let me see. I can't see Sidski Banovci here, I can only see Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I don't need you to go beyond -- the only area we're interested in is Vukovar and then the first place that you stopped on the way out of Vukovar. Can you see the road between Vukovar and Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. We stopped somewhere here on this road, from Vukovar to Negoslavci, but I can't see Negoslavci here. Oh, here's Negoslavci. We stopped somewhere here, somewhere before Negoslavci. We were leaving Vukovar and Negoslavci is here. If you saw what I was pointing at, somewhere around here, before Negoslavci, here. This is the road. This is where we stopped. This is where the settlement is. We joined the column because we could not pass it. So it's somewhere around here. Just before Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you see Negoslavci from where you were, where you pulled up?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we couldn't see anything from the vehicles, but we came there very quickly. There were a lot of people in Negoslavci, because the local people got out to see this column of women, it is primarily women who were leaving, and they were showing three fingers to these women who were on the buses, but the military police stopped us here, just before Negoslavci, we reached Negoslavci very soon, but I couldn't see anything from this column, I couldn't see where precisely I was. So we got into Negoslavci, and I imagine we were just before Negoslavci because we got into Negoslavci very quickly, so we stopped there a bit because these women from Negoslavci wouldn't let the buses get through immediately. I mean, the buses on which these women were that were being transported out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And this place where you stopped before Negoslavci, were there houses in the area? Was it an inhabited area?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. These were fields. There were fields on the side. There weren't any houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we should look at the video for a moment. And I'd ask you to look at it again for us.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If we could just have the very last section starting from 15.36 -- or 15.34, around about that area, right at the very end, the point where the buses are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's the wrong tape. I'm afraid it's the wrong tape. This has to be scrolled back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, may I ask you whether you have many other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm just about finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, before the tape is played, I want you to look very closely at it and see if you can see any houses where the buses are, and also -- well, no, perhaps we'll just start -- just tell me that, whether you can see any houses where the buses are?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I can, but this is obviously Vukovar. This is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There's no houses at this point. You see that.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no houses. No houses. Now the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You see that building behind there -- perhaps we can --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw -- I saw a house, but I couldn't see that from the buses because I was on the other side of the bus. I was trying to overtake the column. It's possible that that was the very beginning of Negoslavci, it's quite possible. We did not turn anywhere, I mean, from the road from Vukovar to Negoslavci, we didn't stop anywhere until the police asked us to join the column because we had tried to overtake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This isn't Ovcara, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't even know where Ovcara is. It isn't on that road. I've never been to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You noticed from the video that we just saw, there is the last houses from Vukovar, as you left Vukovar, and then this place you said you stopped.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing any houses from the edge of Vukovar and this place? Did you remember seeing any houses on the road between those two places?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't see any houses and I don't think that there are any houses there until Negoslavci, not that I think so, I'm sure that there aren't any houses there along the road. It's a clearing. Before Negoslavci, I think that there was a brigade there with Howitzers, I don't know, perhaps I saw that. But nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The first houses you come to after you leave Vukovar, the first houses --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: After Vukovar, the first houses are Negoslavci, I'm sorry, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, no. I would just like to be clear on one point. Mr. Cvetkovic keeps saying that he was the President of Svetzarevo and then of Jagodina. It's the same town, you know.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I explained that. That's no problem. I explained that, that the town of Jagodina used to be called Svetozarevo, and then when I became President, we changed the name back to the old name, Jagodina. It was in existence as Jagodina for seven hundred years before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This was just by way of clarification. Nothing else, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I have a point which -- on which you may clarify the matters. If I am --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Tell me if I am correct. You said that the meeting at Backa Palanka was attended by another President of the Municipal Assembly whom you forgot to bring with you to Vukovar so that he remained at Ilok. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was Aleksic, President of the Assembly of Vrsac. He was in uniform and he was with the reservists in Ilok, and he asked us to ask his commander whether he could come with us and we forgot, so he stayed behind in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you where Vrsac is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Vrsac is in Banate, at the southern part towards Romania.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In your view, why did he wear a military uniform? He was a political --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: He was also a reservist. I think that he was mobilised because he's a young man. I think he was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much. Any objection to the witness being released? Thank you so much for giving evidence in court. You may be released. And we now take a 20-minute break. --- Recess at 3.33 p.m. --- Resumed at 3.52 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. May I ask you to make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Tomasevic, did the investigator from my office, Miro Zaric (phoen), talk to you?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please take a look? Is this the statement that you signed and can you identify it as your statement?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: With pleasure.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D78, and the English translation, D78A.

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the statement that I signed and that I gave to Investigator Zaric (phoen).

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If there are no objections, I suggest that it be marked as Defence Exhibit number 78?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry. For the sake of procedure, there are two technical errors here, and I told your investigators about it when I talked to them in Belgrade. "Witness Statement." It says: "I was employed in Prijepolje from 1983 until --" it's supposed to say 1997 rather than 1994, as it does here, "and from '94 to '97, I was also the acting director. Also, I did my military service in Belgrade from November 19" -- it is 1984 until October 1985. I know that because I have a copy of the statement in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If there are no objections to this corrected statement, I suggest that it be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you complete the faculty of political science in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where were you employed after that?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: After that, I was employed in Poljemje (phoen) in Prijepolje, as a journalist. That is where I live, and I said that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you there in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I first saw him -- it was the first and only time I saw him that day in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you see him here somewhere in this room?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the gentleman over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So for the first time in your life you saw him on the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On the 20th of November, 1991, why were you in Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: A few days before that, I was in Belgrade, and I talked on the telephone with my colleague and friend, Mr. Jevtovic from Kladovo, and he told me that on that day, he and a group of people from Kladovo would be travelling to the area of Vukovar in order to take humanitarian aid there. I was guided by professional curiosity, and I asked whether I could accompany them, and they said I could. And the next morning, very early, I joined them on this journey in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In front of the Hotel Slavija?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please play the beginning of the tape now, Defence tape, the part from Backa Palanka, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you see yourself, could you please tell us? Could you please stop the tape? Could I please ask the usher to show these photographs to the witness, to Witness Tomasevic, to identify himself, if he is in these photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D79.

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is that photograph. It is framed from the videotape that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please continue playing the tape now? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you see yourself, please show me again where you are.

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Stop. This is where I am, in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please play the tape a bit more? Then -- ah, yes, you can see better now. Yes. Stop. Thank you. Could I ask the usher to show these photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D80.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If there are no objections, could this please be admitted into evidence as a Defence Exhibit? Both photographs, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you recognise the faces in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm at the right. Next to me is Mr. Boris, a journalist from Radio Kladovo, then Mr. Lazarevic, Nebojsa Lazarevic, President of the Municipal Assembly of Kladovo, and the gentleman who is in front, I don't know his name, but I think that at that time he was a Member of Parliament from Kladovo in the Parliament of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember where you went afterwards from Backa Palanka and with whom?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From Backa Palanka, the group that I was with set out for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was in this group?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: In this group, there was I and a gentleman called Mirko Dragisic and a gentleman whose last name is Ivezic, I think, the driver of the Municipal Assembly of Kladovo, then Mr. Jovan Cvetkovic, Mr. Dokmanovic, Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Zoran Jevtovic, and Mr. Rade Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You took two cars, I imagine, because there were quite a few of you, it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I think that at one point we even had three cars for one leg of the journey, but after that, I was in one car, and Mr. Dragisic were the driver, Slavko, that driver from the municipal assembly of Kladovo. In the other car, a red Lada Niva, were -- Mr. Cvetkovic was driving, Mr. Dokmanovic, Mr. Lazarevic, and Mr. Jevtovic. In the third car, I think it was a Mercedes, chocolate-coloured Mercedes, was Mr. Leskovac, but his car broke down somewhere along the road, and then he also moved into the Lada that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you following this car all the time, I mean the red Lada Niva?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you arrived in Vukovar, did you arrive at the same time?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does that mean that -- does that mean that at the same time when you arrived with your car that Slavko Dokmanovic arrived with his car too?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you saw him all the way, I mean, from Backa Palanka to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: He was within eyesight, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you arrived in Vukovar, where did you stop first?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: This is as far as I can remember, on the outskirts of Vukovar. It was the yard of a company. VELEPROMET, it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you passed the gate, when you enter the compound of VELEPROMET, was Slavko Dokmanovic with you?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did you do in VELEPROMET during that period of time that you spent there, and do you know what Slavko Dokmanovic did during that time?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: We were in the part of the yard that is immediately after this metal gate that was opened. Our group that came was there, and there were some other people there too. I didn't know them and I didn't know who they were or what they were. We were looking around, we were talking to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know where Slavko Dokmanovic was at that time?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: For a certain period of time, Slavko was with us, and then he got into a building which was on the right-hand side, it was to the right of the gate where we entered the place, from the street; and a meeting, some kind of meeting, was taking place in this building, and Mr. Dokmanovic attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what happened when Mr. Dokmanovic came back? Did you see him when he came back?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were waiting for him to come out, and we spent a few more minutes there at that same position at the entrance into the yard, and then we got into our cars again, and we went well into the town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like to have the tape played now, please, and could you show us whether this is what you said? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's it. Please watch the tape and see whether that's it. If you see yourself, please show us.

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was filmed as we were entering Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Stop. Would you please tell us who is on the picture and what they are doing?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: This is me and Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just one moment, please. I would like the witness to be shown these photographs. This is part 80?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We will wait for the judges to look at the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who is on the photograph and what is happening at that time?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The photograph, and before that on the tape, are depicted myself and Mr. Dokmanovic. I used a moment, the stop that we made at an intersection there in Vukovar, to take a statement from Mr. Dokmanovic about his impressions about everything that was happening and that we had seen. As a professional journalist, I always carried in my bag a small reporter's tape recorder which I used to take statements for my radio show, so I did this this time with Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did you do in the centre of town when you got there?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: While I was talking with Mr. Dokmanovic, the rest of the group were looking around them. I think we stayed there for a few minutes at that intersection. Then we could hear shots. We could hear, if I remember well, several individual shots and then several more shots, and this was the reason why we turned our vehicles around and sat -- went back into the vehicles and took the same road back to leave the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you remember the impressions of Slavko Dokmanovic in that interview? What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I wouldn't even call that an interview, I would only call that a statement, you know, because of its form -- because of its length, it's not an interview in the classical sense, so it's a statement. I asked Mr. Dokmanovic for his impressions about everything. As far as I remember, he told me that, the first thing, that he was amazed to see what he was seeing because this was the first time he entered the City of Vukovar. He was amazed at the destruction and by the corpses that we saw on the streets, and you could see that on the videotape. He told me that things should not have come to this. Everything could have been resolved in a different way without war, without this unnecessary destruction and the numerous victims. He said that he hoped that this will never happen again anywhere and that the world will draw a lesson from this and will never allow this to happen again. At the end, he expressed the desire, the hope, that Vukovar will remain in Serb hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In his words, was there any desire for revenge? Was there any revengeism [sic] there?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I remember that Mr. Dokmanovic didn't talk about any categories such as hate, conflict, war, and so forth. I think that he spoke generally about the unnecessary human suffering and the unnecessary destruction in destroying the city and the material goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you finished everything, which direction then did you proceed in?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we went back towards the exit to Vukovar, the same way that we came. We took the same way to return, back towards Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So now you're coming back. Who is in which car?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The same composition. In front, there is the Lada Niva that is driven by Mr. Cvetkovic, and Mr. Leskovac, Lazarevic, and Novakovic are there. This is followed by the car of the Kladovo Assembly, which were myself, the driver, and Mirko Dragisic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I understood properly, the Lada was leading and you were driving behind the Lada, so you could see the Lada in front of you all the way along the road?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we drove one behind another, one car behind another.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you stop anywhere from the time you left Vukovar until you arrived to Sidski Banovci and how many times did you stop?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we stopped twice. On the first occasion, when we arrived, when we overtook the convoy of the buses and the military trucks which was accompanied by the International Red Cross, they were transporting civilians. Then there was a traffic jam on the road, so this is where we stopped. This lasted -- I can't remember exactly -- several minutes, not too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that was the first time. What about the second time?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The second time we stopped at an intersection in a place called Orolik where, once again, there was a traffic jam. There was the column of the buses and the military vehicles. Once again, our vehicles tried to overtake this column, but we came to a barrier which was across the road, and this was manned by the JNA military police. We stopped there. I think we waited for some time and so forth. Then the gentlemen that I described who were in the Lada Niva went out of the vehicle and they went towards the soldiers who were there. As far as I remember and as far as I understood the situation at that time, they wanted the barrier to be raised so that we could pass, so that we didn't have to wait there. There was an incident there, there was a kind of argument between the military police and the group there, and when we saw that, me and the people from my car came out of the vehicle and went towards them, the other group. There were a few other people who got involved as well. There was some cursing and arguments and so on. The situation was resolved in the way that Mr. Cvetkovic, who was a reserve officer of the JNA, used his authority as an officer, so then he kind of mediated for the situation to settle down, and in a way, with his officer's authority, he ensured for the barrier to be raised and then we passed with our vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you remember at what time of the day this was? What was the time and what was the visibility?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: This was already dusk. So at the break, at the change between day and night, visibility was limited in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During your first stop, did Mr. Dokmanovic leave the car; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. None of us left the vehicles during the first stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then at the second stop, what happened? During that journey from Vukovar and up to Orolik and further, did you turn from the road anywhere --

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: -- especially before you got to Orolik?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: After Orolik, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: After, we went to a place called Sidski Banovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I think until maybe 18 hours. It was already night. In one of the houses in the village was the headquarters of the unit commanded by Mr. Cvetkovic. We went there, entered there for refreshments. Myself and Mr. Jevtovic very quickly after that left those premises, we left that location, and the reason was we were told that the bridge between Backa Palanka and the other bank of the Danube closes for traffic at seven o'clock because this was a war zone. I needed to be in Belgrade the next day. Mr. Jevtovic also was in a hurry. And for that reason, we separated from the group. From Mr. Cvetkovic we received a military vehicle and a driver who drove us from Sidski Banovci across the bridge and to the bus depot in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What was the last time when you saw Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I saw him last there in -- on those premises where the headquarters of Mr. Cvetkovic was, and this was around 18 hours, as far as I can recall. I can't be precise about the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he say good-bye to you?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When Mr. Cvetkovic spoke to the JNA people at the Orolik checkpoint, what did he say to them; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said he used his authority as a captain. He was a captain of the region, was he, of that particular area?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say he was a captain. I don't know, really, if he was a captain. In any case, he was a reserve officer. I don't know what his rank was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But in any event, you said that he exercised his authority which cleared up the matter and permitted you to pass?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You then went to the headquarters, Mr. Cvetkovic's headquarters, in Sidski Banovci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And at that place, he ordered that you be given a car to take you back to Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if he ordered, but he did provide a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Going back to the morning of the 20th when you're in Backa Palanka and attended the meeting in Backa Palanka, what was discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't call that a meeting, first of all, because as far as I know, it wasn't an officially scheduled, organised gathering. They discussed different things, and from the time distance, I can't really be specific or quote anything from there, but I think mostly the current political situation was discussed, what was happening in that area and so forth, and also other things were being talked about, of course. We were there for a couple of hours in that office, so I can't really be specific about what was spoken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about the proposed government meeting in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any discussion as to what would happen in Vukovar now that the war was over?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about what would happen to Vukovar now that the attack on Vukovar had been completed?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you make any notes of this meeting? Was it of any newsworthy value so far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't take notes at that time because my intention was not to go there in order to gather news. I'm a journalist in a local newspaper house and it's far away from that region, so that I didn't even have the technical capability to broadcast news or it wasn't something that was interesting to my listeners. My intention was different. I wanted to see something there and then later, my impressions, to publish them in the form of a report in a local paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you understand why the meeting took place, whether it be informal or otherwise? Do you understand why those men were gathered there?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I think because it was the last place before the entry into the war zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why was it necessary for them to gather there for that reason?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't reply to that. I can't be any more specific than what I've already stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did you go to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I tried to explain that before. As a journalist, I was interested to see with my eyes what really happened -- what's really happening there because before, earlier information that I had about that was through the media, and as I said, since I was presented with this opportunity, my original plan was to try to make a report, a feature, from the war zone. Because previously, once before, I was on the front during the events in Dubrovnik, and then after that, I wrote a very nice feature. When I say "nice," I mean from the journalistic aspect, very good quality feature from that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you, why did you go to the meeting at Backa Palanka? Why did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Simply, all the people that I was in the group with, they went, entered that building. What else could I do? I went with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know why they were going to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were driving -- taking humanitarian aid there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the humanitarian aid go with you, in the group of people that went with you? Did they take humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: The group that was taking the humanitarian aid separated in Backa Palanka. One group of people and the truck with the aid left to a different destination where, as far as I know, were reservists from Kladovo. This group, comprising the people that I've already mentioned, went to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, but the group of people that you went with to Vukovar either didn't go there for the purposes of providing aid or, alternatively, they became separated. Can you clarify what happened for us?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I can't really explain that specifically, if you're asking me why did I go with this group and not with the other group. I went with this group because of all of those people, I only knew Mr. Lazarevic and Mr. Jevtovic, so it's quite logical that I would go with them and I would not be separated from them and not to go with people that I saw for the first time in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You didn't travel with Mr. Dokmanovic in the same vehicle at any stage, did you?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived at Vukovar, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I already said that earlier. If I need to repeat it, I will repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: When we got to Vukovar, we entered into the yard of this company, VELEPROMET. I said that we were there -- at the beginning of the yard, it was quite a big yard, we were there for a while, maybe an hour, approximately, and then we went down into the town until the place where I spoke with Mr. Dokmanovic, and then we came back, as I already described.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see Arkan at this place?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't directly talk to him the way I'm speaking directly with you, it wasn't a dialogue between myself and Arkan, but the whole group that I was with talked to him. They talked with Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see any JNA officers there?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Where do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: VELEPROMET.

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know who they were?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: You mean by name?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you recognise any rank?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that, really. It's a detail that wasn't important to me at that moment, and a lot of time has passed since then, so I can't remember. But it's true that there were officers and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, a government meeting took place at VELEPROMET when you were there?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: That's what we were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you endeavour to find out what the meeting was about?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As a journalist, wouldn't it have been of some interest to you, to know what the meeting that was taking place was about?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. You know, I was aware of my position as journalist at that moment. Before me, there were journalists there already and they came from major publishing, media houses, and they were reporting from that region, they were giving information and news, so there was no need for me to look for something exclusive or any other kind of news.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So how long did you stay there while the meeting was on?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe about an hour. You can see that from the timing, by analysing the videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Dokmanovic came out of the meeting, did he speak to you or to a group of people there?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: You mean at the end of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, really. It was a normal story. We didn't really discuss anything in particular there in order for that to remain in my mind so that I would remember that after so many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, Goran Hadzic was there too, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He gave an interview to the media, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he gave an interview, I think for French television. I know the gentleman who interviewed him, his name is Zoran Petrovic Pirocanac. He was known to me from before, not personally, but I knew of him as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, did you ascertain what Goran Hadzic had said to the media?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was of no interest to you?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dokmanovic didn't come from your area, did he? He came from the Vukovar area.

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did you choose to interview him in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I think because he was the only person in that group from that area, you know. It wasn't interesting to me, and I think it would be unprofessional to ask Mr. Lazarevic or somebody else who came from Kladovo for their impressions because their impressions would be identical -- could only be identical to mine, to the things that I felt. So a different impression could be only from somebody who was a local, who was from there, and that could only come from Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, after you left Vukovar, where did you go? Describe the route that you followed, if you would for me, once you left the centre of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: We came back the same way that we entered the city, and then on the way out, we passed the building of VELEPROMET again, and then, as I said, we took the same way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you stop at VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: On our return?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I think that we didn't. As far as I remember, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the other vehicle stop?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. Because this vehicle was ahead of us. If they had stopped, then we would have had to stop too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It never stopped at any stage, even momentarily, after you left the centre of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, until the situation that I described when we caught up with the convoy, with the civilians, we did not stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the specific location because I'm not really -- I'm not from that region. But it was on the road, on the return from Vukovar towards Sidski Banovci, towards Backa Palanka; of course, on some road somewhere between Vukovar and this Orolik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you reached Sidski Banovci, what happened there that night? What happened to the group? It split up, did it?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that myself and Mr. Jevtovic spent a very short time there, and then we left Sidski Banovci and that whole region. What happened then there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you understand that the rest of the people were going to stay there the night, or were they to travel later on?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I can't reply to that at this moment, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I forgot a question. It's not very important, but still ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you receive this videotape that we showed you just now? From whom did you get it and when and do you still have it?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I received a copy of this videotape a few days or maybe a few weeks after our stay in Vukovar. I received it by mail from Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you have it at home?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have that tape at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So if the court requested it, would you be able to submit it?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I already talked to the gentleman that I spoke to in Belgrade that I was willing to give that tape, if necessary, but nobody said that I needed to bring it with me here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Tomasevic, I wonder whether you could help us by answering two questions? First of all, did you make any use of the statement given to you by Mr. Dokmanovic? You remember, you said you interviewed him. Did you use it, this interview, for an article, a feature from the war zone, for your own notes? Did you keep the tape?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No, unfortunately, I didn't keep that tape for the simple reason because it's what we call "working tape." It's a tape that you keep and you use it and then you rewind it and you record over it. So the practice, at least in the newsroom where I work, that if something is estimated as important, then you would archive it on a different tape. So there is a special way to archive everything. I didn't really give any importance to that statement, so then I re-recorded that statement, I didn't keep it or the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In addition, you didn't use that tape or the statement, the actual statement made by Mr. Dokmanovic, for an article feature? I wonder whether you did use it.

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I did not use that statement. To my regret, I didn't write that text that I wanted to write when I returned about my visit to Vukovar. When I came back to the place where I live and work, I tried several nights to describe what I lived through in Vukovar, what I experienced in Vukovar, but unfortunately, I didn't have the strength, the concentration, or the power to put everything that I saw there into a newspaper article. And then for the same reason, the local newspaper that I worked for at that time, I published only a photo report about Vukovar. The next day, on my return from Vukovar, I knew that if I wanted to write this article, I would need photographs, so for that reason, I went to the newsroom of the Politika publishing house where I used to work for a few years as a journalist and I knew a lot of people there, some colleagues from my university worked there, and there are a lot of photo journalists there. I know one of them who I met there. So he took photographs for Politika in the Vukovar region. I took several photographs, and I wanted to publish them together with the text that I wanted to write, but since I didn't find a way to write this text, I -- on half a page of newspaper that I worked for, I just published those photographs under the headline "Vukovar" without any other comment or without a signature, and that is the only trace of my visit to Vukovar which remains in the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. My second and last question is about what you said in your written statement. At one point, you saw quite a few dead bodies. This was before you asked Mr. Dokmanovic to give you an interview, to make a statement. And you saw quite a few dead bodies and you said "which were slaughtered and their eyes were forcefully taken out. All of us went out of the car and we saw the scene." Probably these were corpses or bodies other than the ones we saw on the videotape. I wonder whether at that stage you could realise whether or not these were bodies of military personnel or civilians, the corpses you saw and which struck you?

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, but I have to intervene. Perhaps this statement was not precise enough. When I was describing the number of people -- I mean, it was just what was registered on the tape. I was just saying that I see what the tape is recording, but I don't know -- I didn't know then and I don't know now what kind of people they were. It was a terrible sight, at least for me personally. It was the first time in my life that I had seen a killed person, a person with their throat slit, with their skulls broken, with their eyes -- they were forcefully taken out. So there were several corpses there in the street. It is not that we felt any need to identify the corpses or anything. I was astounded by what I saw. And at that point in time, I didn't have any reason to ascertain what kind of corpses these were and who these people were, you know, if you understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So at that stage you didn't see whether -- or identify the bodies. You were unable to say whether they were military people or civilians or Serbs or Croats; just dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: VUKOSAV TOMASEVIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, and we can see the tape once again, but I think that they were civilians, and even on a living person -- you know, in our country, they say -- it doesn't say on your forehead what nationality you belong in, and least of all if a person is dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So I assume there's no objection to the witness being released? Mr. Tomasevic, thank you so much for coming here to give evidence in court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (Witness stands down)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I will now turn to Mr. Fila and ask him whether he has skipped the third witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, because the cross-examination of the Prosecutor is so long, I thought that we wouldn't have enough time for the other witness. Lazarevic is a longer witness, so I thought that we would finish today with three witnesses altogether because otherwise it would have been two and a half witnesses, so to speak. So perhaps I can start with Lazarevic in these ten minutes, if you wish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, no, no. Actually, I think it was a good idea. So I meant to ask you whether you are going to call tomorrow Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. Your Honour, it's only Lazarevic and another one that are a bit longer, for your information, really, so that you would know what lies in store. And the remaining four will only take about 15 minutes or so. I don't believe that Mr. Niemann will question them much longer either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. So we now can take our recess, and we will reconvene tomorrow at 9.00 a.m. sharp.
